articles.title: All smiles in Strasbourg but uncertainty clouds Canada’s EU membership plan
articles.summary: Although Mark Carney welcomed offer to become bloc’s first associate member, no one seems to know what that means

blocks.text: Mark Carney received a rapturous reception in the European parliament when he gave his speech on Thursday welcoming a proposal for Canada to become the EU’s first-ever associate member.

Politicians queued to shake his hand and take selfies. One MEP leader described the speech as a historic moment. “Europe has extended a hand, and Canada has taken it,” said the German Green MEP Terry Reintke, who borrowed a Canadian ice hockey shirt for the occasion.

One day earlier, in the same debating chamber, the European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, issued the unprecedented invitation to Canada to become an associate member – an idea quickly derided by Donald Trump, who threatened Europe with “heavy tariffs” if it became a reality.

But the prospect of Canada’s associate membership is uncertain, not least because no one is sure what it means. “I’m not quite sure why she [von der Leyen] used that term because there’s simply no legal definition,” said one senior politician. “This has just raised lots of questions. So people are talking more about what an associate membership means instead of … this unique partnership and alliance for the future that EU-Canada relations should be about.”

The German chancellor Friedrich Merz’s spokesperson welcomed the initiative for a close partnership with Canada and said Germany was “open to discussing new models that reflect the special significance of the relationship” but called for the associate membership label to be “reconsidered”.
Merz himself has floated “associate membership” for Ukraine, as a stepping stone to joining the bloc, but this was quickly dismissed by other member states.

One EU diplomat said von der Leyen “seemed a bit far out in floating this” and that even before Wednesday’s speech member states had worried that she was overpromising on Canada. A second diplomat said it was “an empty phrase” and it would be up to member states to define the substance.
Any new trading and cooperation relationship with a foreign country would need to be approved by the EU’s 27 member states.

There is a lot of common ground: both sides want to deepen cooperation on AI, energy security, critical raw materials, quantum computing and work together in the Arctic – Carney noted that Canada shared an Arctic border with Denmark, referring to the maritime border with Greenland.

But difficulties went unspoken. While Carney described the 2016 EU-Canada comprehensive economic and trade agreement as “one of the world’s most successful trade agreements”, 10 EU member states have yet to ratify it, including France, Italy and Poland. With all three countries heading into an election year, that looks unlikely to change.

While both sides extol the virtues of deeper trade between allies, they are also pursuing policies that appear to contradict that goal. Last year Canada introduced a buy Canadian policy, to ensure Canadian suppliers get priority in public contracts. The EU is debating its own buy European law, known formally as the Industrial Accelerator Act. The IAA, now being debated in the EU, would oblige member states to meet “made in Europe” content requirements when spending public money on green technologies and electric cars.

Associate membership also raises questions about integration into the EU’s tightly guarded single market. Carney proposed “seamless digital trade in non-agricultural goods and a wide range of services”. But the EU has long insisted that the four freedoms of its internal market – free movement of goods, services, labour and capital – are one package that cannot be split and require alignment with EU rules.
Now the applause has died down, there are plenty of tricky issues to work out, even for the closest of allies.

articles.title: Montenegro Lines bans EVs and HEVs on vessels as safety precaution
articles.summary: Domestic shipping company Montenegro Lines announced that it is banning, "effective immediately," any electric vehicle (EV) or hybrid EV (HEV) from its vessels, whether for passenger or cargo…

blocks.text: Published September 17, 2026 11:42pm

Domestic shipping company Montenegro Lines announced that it is banning, "effective immediately," any electric vehicle (EV) or hybrid EV (HEV) from its vessels, whether for passenger or cargo carriage, as a safety measure.

"This measure is being implemented as a preventive safety precaution to minimize the risk of fire, explosion, thermal runaway, and other potential hazards associated with electric and hybrid vehicle batteries during vessel operations," the shipping line said.

Earlier in the day, the Department of Energy said that authorities are working to soon issue safety regulations on the transportation of EVs following the deadly fire that broke out aboard the MV June Aster while it was sailing to Coron, Palawan.
The department said it is already coordinating with the Maritime Industry Authority.
In a statement, Montenegro Lines also directed its Vessel Masters to enforce the following:
Ensure that no electric or hybrid vehicle is accepted for boarding or carriage onboard
Coordinate with the Operations Department, Terminal, Ticketing, Loading, and Cargo Personnel to ensure strict implementation of this directive
Ensure that vehicles are properly identified and checked prior to boarding:
Immediately report any attempted boarding or carriage of an electric or hybrid vehicle to the Operations Department and SQA Department
Strictly comply with this directive until further notice or until Management issues a revised instruction

"The safety and protection of our passengers, crew, vessels, and cargo remain our highest priority. All concerned personnel are expected to exercise vigilance and ensure strict compliance with this directive," it said.

Montenegro Shipping Lines Inc. is a domestic shipping company in the Philippines that was established in 1978 with initial routes from Batangas City to Mindoro Island and vice versa. articles.summary: Five people were reportedly killed as the escalation between the two sides continues to spiral. The Houthis denied attacking Mecca, with Saudi Arabia saying one person was killed by drone shrapnel.

image.caption: Damage was caused to buildings and cars in Saudi ArabiaImage: SPA/AFP

blocks.text: At least five people were killed in the escalation between the Iran-backed Houthirebel group and the internationally recognized Yemeni government, supported by Saudi Arabia.
Saudi Arabia accused the Houthis of a "cowardly" strike on Mecca, the holiest city in Islam and the site of the hajj and umrah pilgrimages, this week.
The rebel group denied the accusations.
Meanwhile, the Houthis claimed Saudi warplanes targeted three telecommunication towers in Taiz in southwestern Yemen.

According to the Almisrah TV channel, backed by the Houthis, one civilian was killed in the town of Abs in the northwest, with the channel later reporting that three children were killed by strikes carried out by Yemen's internationally recognized government.
In Saudi Arabia, one person was killed by shrapnel from a downed drone in the Mecca area, the country's civil defense agency said. Damage was also caused to buildings and vehicles.
This was the first reported death in Saudi Arabia in the current escalation between the two sides.

blocks.caption: Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces are fighting against the HouthisImage: AFP

blocks.text: Important strait taken over

The truce between the Houthis and Saudi Arabia, agreed on in 2022, collapsed in July after the Iran-backed group allowed an Iranian plane to land in Yemen's capital Sanaa, which defied the Saudis' control over Yemeni airspace. As a result of the escalation, the Houthis announced a maritime blockade on Saudi Arabia.
The Houthis have controlled Sanaa and much of Yemen's more populous western areas since the start of Yemen's civil war in 2014.

The rebel group has reported dozens of Saudi strikes since its recent offensive to secure control over the coastal areas near the Red Sea's Bab al-Mandab Strait, one of the world's most important shipping routes, from government hands.
The strait's importance has increased since Iran put restrictions on the Strait of Hormuz over the US and Israel's war with Tehran.
The conflict in Yemen has forced more than 100,000 people to flee their homes, according to UN figures.

articles.title: House Republican releases campaign ad critical of Trump’s immigration policies
articles.summary:
María Elvira Salazar says some enforcement has ‘gone too far’ as GOP seeks distance from Trump before midterms

A Republican…

blocks.text: A Republican congresswoman has released a campaign ad criticizing Donald Trump’s approach to immigration enforcement, in the latest sign that a key plank of the president’s 2024 re-election campaign has become a liability for his congressional allies ahead of November’s midterm elections.

“Mr. President, some of your immigration enforcement efforts have gone too far,” Florida’s María Elvira Salazar says in a 30-second ad. “In July, 50% of the 50,000 people that were detained had no criminal record. Be careful what your advisers are telling you about immigration policy.”

Salazar represents a competitive Miami-area district that is nearly three-quarters Hispanic, and where Trump won by a 15-percentage point margin two years ago after a campaign in which he promised to carry out “mass deportations”. While his administration has implied that those targeted would be undocumented immigrants who committed crimes in the United States, in reality, a substantial portion of the people arrested since Trump returned to the White House in January 2025 have no criminal record.

Salazar won re-election by a 20 percentage point margin in 2024 but this year is facing a significant challenge from Eliott Rodriguez, the Democratic nominee and a former television news anchor. A poll conducted for his campaign late last month found him tied with Salazar.
after newsletter promotion

“The same Hispanics who helped you get to the White House in 2024 feel betrayed today,” Salazar said in the ad. “You can be for immigration what Lincoln was for slavery and Reagan was for communism. I’m not talking about giving them amnesty. I’m talking about giving them a dignified life in this promised land.”

First elected in 2020, the congresswoman is a champion of the Dignity Act, an immigration reform proposal in the House of Representatives that would create a pathway for some undocumented immigrants to obtain legal status.

Salazar’s ad is the latest instance of Republican lawmakers seeking to put distance between themselves and Trump ahead of the 3 November elections, in which Democrats are vying to take back both the House and Senate. With gas prices high due to the war with Iran and Trump’s public approval low – including on key issues like handling of immigration – Democrats increasingly believe their candidates are competitive even in heavily Republican seats.

articles.title: Sweden’s PM resigns after centre-left bloc wins slim majority in election
articles.summary:
Ulf Kristersson has stood down from his post, paving way for Social Democrats leader to form a government

Sweden’s centre-right prime…

blocks.text: Sweden’s centre-right prime minister, Ulf Kristersson, has stood down, clearing the way for Magdalena Andersson, the Social Democrats leader, to attempt to form a government.
In a victory speech on Thursday, Andersson said the Swedish people had “voted for a new direction for our country, voted for unity and against division”.
She added: “The Swedish people have voted to take Sweden forward and I will realise the new direction that you have voted for.”
Among the priorities she named were the climate crisis, schools, healthcare, elderly care and immigration policy.

Andersson spoke as the preliminary count for Sunday’s election was finally completed, with 176 seats for the left-leaning opposition parties – a narrow three-seat majority over the right-leaning ruling Tidö coalition supported by the far-right Sweden Democrats (SD). There were 50,359 votes between the two blocs.
Earlier on Thursday, Andersson, who was Kristersson’s predecessor as prime minister, sent an invitation to the other left-leaning parties – Left, Centre and Green – for initial coalition talks.
Soon after, Kristersson, the Moderates leader, announced his resignation after four years as prime minister.

Before the election, some had feared that the vote would mark a turning point for the far right after Kristersson promised key ministerial posts for the SD if his coalition took power. Instead, the SD lost support for the first time in a general election since its foundation, falling from Sweden’s second biggest party to third.

In his resignation letter, Kristersson wrote: “Now it is the speaker who will lead the next steps towards forming a new government. In order for that work to begin immediately, I hereby request to be relieved of my duties as prime minister.”
The speaker, Andreas Norlén, will now start working on proposals for a new prime minister after talks with representatives of each of the parties.

blocks.caption: Magdalena Andersson claps on stage as the general election results are released in Stockholm, Sweden. Photograph: Denis Balibouse/Reuters

blocks.text: Four celebration cakes decorated with red roses were brought into the Social Democrats’ headquarters amid cheers from inside.

The result will be a considerable relief among Social Democrats, who remain Sweden’s biggest party but received record low support. However, the result marks only the beginning for Andersson of what is expected to be weeks of complicated coalition talks.

One of the trickiest negotiations is expected to be between the Centre and Left parties. The Centre party has ruled out being in government with the Left, while the Left has demanded a place in government in return for its cooperation.

Other difficult areas are expected to be the Left’s support for a billionaire tax, the Green party’s opposition to nuclear energy and differences of opinion on taxation. The Greens, Social Democrats and the Left are all in favour of tax increases, but the Centre party wants to cut taxes.
after newsletter promotion
Nooshi Dadgostar, the leader of the Left party, said: “The Swedish people have voted away Tidö and given us a clear mandate for change.” She added: “This is one of the proudest days of my life.”

Elisabeth Thand Ringqvist, the Centre party leader, thanked Kristersson for his work as prime minister but said Sweden was now “entering a new political phase”. She added: “The Centre party will be a constructive force for Sweden to have a functioning government, with policies anchored in the middle.”

Andersson, who was prime minister between November 2021 and October 2022, is understood to be reaching out to all the opposition parties, with the exception of the SD. The Liberals and the Christian Democrats have ruled out working with the left, but in his resignation letter Kristersson appeared to leave the door open. However, given Swedish tradition, it is extremely unlikely the Moderates and the Social Democrats would form a coalition.
Kristersson wrote that the election had left a “complicated situation” for building a government and called for “constructive openness” from all parties to find a way to form a stable government.

In the nervous days since the election, the Social Democrats are understood to have been using the time to prepare for coalition negotiations, where they are understood to be seeking broad cooperation with one or multiple parties.

Minority-run governments are common within Swedish politics and it is commonplace for governments to form agreements outside of coalitions. In the last government, the SD were not officially in government, but they held considerable sway over the budget and policies.

The Social Democrats are understood to be planning to prioritise making changes to the immigration, integration and climate policies of the last government. But with their policies having moved to the right in recent years, particularly on immigration and crime, much of the legacy of the previous government is likely to remain.

articles.title: Germany's judges seek to prevent AfD justice abuse
articles.summary: German judges and prosecutors have warned that the government needs to reform the laws around how state prosecutors to prevent extremist parties like the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD)…

image.caption: German judges want to make sure state governments cannot abuse prosecution powers to influence criminal casesImage: Jennifer Brückner/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: The official association of German judges, the Deutscher Richterbund (DRB), has called on the federal government to tighten up the law to stop state governments from abusing prosecution powers to potentially influence criminal cases.

The prospect of the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) taking over the government in Saxony-Anhalt, which appears highly likely after the party's resounding election win in early September, has raised fears that "extremists in government" could steer "criminal investigations in one direction or another through directives," according to the DRB.

The AfD, sections of which are considered a threat to the German constitutional democratic order by domestic intelligence agencies, is set to take control of a government for the first time ever in Saxony-Anhalt. This has sparked concern in the judicial system that the party could, for instance, push prosecutors away from pursuing cases against right-wing extremists.

"The top priority now is to prevent the misuse of public prosecutors' offices in Germany for partisan political purposes," DRB executive director Sven Rebehn said in a statement emailed to DW. "Currently, the law allows state justice ministries to interfere even in individual criminal proceedings. While there is a political tradition of self-restraint when issuing directives to prosecutors, this tradition can be abandoned at any time and offers no effective protection."
New report backs ban of German far-right party
State prosecutors — not independent

In Germany, unlike in many other countries, state prosecutors, along with the police, are part of the executive branch of government. This puts them under the authority of the state or federal Interior Ministries, and subject to parliamentary oversight. This dependence is seen by many constitutional lawyers as a democratic principle, as it means that prosecutors' actions can be checked by a democratically elected body. But others see it as a problem, as it opens the possibility of political influence.

German Interior Ministries, both at the federal level and in the 16 states, have the power to issue directives to prosecutors in individual cases. For instance, if some evidence has been supplied by an intelligence agency, the Interior Ministry can issue a directive to the prosecutor to keep that fact out of a court case, as disclosing it could compromise the work of the agency.

The German domestic intelligence agency, the Verfassungsschutz, which reports to the Interior Ministry, has long been a focus of the AfD's ire, as they consider it politicized. The agency is charged with keeping tabs on extremist tendencies in the country. By the same token, German Justice Ministries can make a ruling over how prosecutors interpret a certain law, or how investigations are to be pursued.

One such controversial directive was made in 2015, when the then federal Justice Minister Heiko Maas told the federal prosecutor to withdraw a report that found that state secrets had been compromised in a particular case. Maas denied that this had been the directive, and federal prosecutor Harald Range was dismissed in the ensuing power struggle.

As things stand, there is still no way to check the ministry's directives, which some see as a problem. Berlin's state prosecutor, Margarete Koppers, also has strong opinions on this point, and sees the danger as acute: "The rule of law is at risk when its rules are politically abused," a spokesperson for Koppers told DW by email. "A look at European countries that have, at various times, been under authoritarian-populist leadership — and where the structures of the rule of law were subsequently eroded — shows that this is not an unrealistic scenario." When the far-right Law and Justice (PiS) party took over in Poland, it triggered a constitutional crisis by trying to appoint judges to the constitutional court. The government of Viktor Orban in Hungary also tried to intervene in the judicial system.
EU, Poland row over judicial committee
Another option: Make directives transparent
Both the DRB and Koppers believe removing the ministries' right to take directives is long overdue, but others in the judicial community are not so sure.

"I can understand the fear that a sword like this in the hands of the wrong people makes the executive branch a danger," said Gül Pinar, a criminal lawyer based in Hamburg who in 2020 offered expert testimony in the Bundestag on the issue.

But Pinar agrees that reform is necessary, but mainly because ministries' directives are not documented. "The people who are affected by the criminal procedures don't know that certain actions taken by the prosecutors stem from a directive, from the government, or the federal prosecutors, or the Interior Ministry," she told DW.

But if the directives were documented, Pinar argued, it would be possible for lawyers to examine whether they were legally sound, or whether they overstepped their authority. "We have to insert new mechanisms to check what is happening," she said.

"But the solution is not to make the state prosecutors independent," she underlined. Hardly anyone in the judiciary, Pinar said, doubts that the right to issue instructions stems from the principle of democracy. But she added that there were many voices, particularly amongst judges and public prosecutors, who advocate for an independent public prosecution service.

For its part, the current federal government has not shown any inclination to change the law. In a statement to the Legal Tribune Online, the Federal Justice Ministry said that the current laws provided plenty of safeguards: Ministries are prohibited from issuing "unlawful" directives, and prosecutors from following them.
In fact, the ministry said, keeping prosecutors as part of the executive branch was important, because it meant that they were more accountable and subject to parliamentary oversight.
Inside the AfD
The European arrest warrant problem

The relatively unique position of Germany's state prosecutors has come up at the European level before: In 2019, the European Court of Justice warned that European arrest warrants could be compromised by political influence because German state prosecutors were not independent enough — while European arrest warrants are supposed to be issued by state prosecutors, in Germany, only judges are allowed issue them.

According to Pinar, allowing state prosecutors to issue arrest warrants is "not compatible with our legal system." In fact, she thinks the German system safeguards more civil freedoms: "In Germany, withdrawing someone's freedom is always under the authority of the judge," she said. "I think it would better if other countries adapted their systems to ours, so that the executive branch can decide on the freedom, but was under a judge's authority."
Edited by Rina Goldenberg

articles.title: Amid claims of ‘mass migration’, Labor hopes a measured approach will take the hot air out of the debate
articles.summary:
The country’s migration settings have become a source of discontent – but will Tony Burke’s approach be seen as the right mix?

  • Get our

blocks.text: Tony Burke has promised to make Labor’s existing migration policy work better rather than announcing a dramatic cut in numbers, arguing that populist promises to slash net overseas migration will “trash Australian services and trash the Australian economy”.

The home affairs minister’s message was immediately endorsed by employer groups, who over recent days have made it clear that steps to arbitrarily slash migrant numbers would compound already severe skills shortages and hurt businesses, especially those in the regions.

“We need immigration. We just need to make sure that it is targeted for the needs of Australia in numbers and across the different categories that work for our economy,” Burke said in his long-awaited address to the National Press Club on Thursday.

“We talk about the need for extra housing. It’s pretty hard to get a house built without having a plasterer involved. In both Sydney and Melbourne, close to two-thirds of the plasterers we have were born overseas.”

Bran Black, the chief executive of the Business Council in Australia, welcomed the government’s efforts to “restore integrity to the migration system”, even as he argued against new rules that would limit the length of stay for most backpackers.
“The starting point for migration policy should not be a number to cut to, but what our economy genuinely needs,” Black said.

“Almost one in three occupations in this country are short of workers right now. That translates to not enough workers building homes, caring for us in hospitals and aged care homes, delivering infrastructure and powering the energy transition. That is the challenge that any migration policy should be looking to solve.”

Labor has taken a long time to come up with its policy prescription to fix the country’s migration settings which, after the post-pandemic surge in new arrivals, have become a source of growing popular discontent.

Spurious claims of “mass migration” have fanned the flames of this discontent, but few would argue that our system is working well and in the best interests of the country – or in the best interests of a ballooning number of people trapped in a kind of temporary visa limbo that has strained public infrastructure and patience.

Alan Gamlen, the director of the ANU’s migration hub, said Burke appeared to have announced the right mix of measures that would give the government the capacity to regulate an out-of-control temporary visa system without damaging the economy.
“They don’t seem to have fallen into the trap of chasing a net migration number,” Gamlen said.

“Burke made it pretty clear, and in a convincing way, that this is the result of a well-considered process that has been going on for a while and which addresses long-term structural issues, rather than just a kneejerk response to One Nation.”
One Nation has committed to lowering net overseas migration to 130,000 a year, and the Coalition somewhere between 150,000 and 170,000.
In comparison, Burke stuck to the government’s forecast of 225,000 people by 2027-28.
He did, however, acknowledge that there was now a public expectation that the government would pull the levers necessary to get there.
after newsletter promotion
“Net overseas migration has been viewed as a budget forecast. Last couple of years, people have talked about it as a budget target,” he said.

“That is a very different way of looking at it. But given that we have the challenges we have with housing in Australia at the moment, I do think we need to be able to have these additional tools to make sure that what is published and forecast is reached.”

With business groups already suffering from skills shortages even at a time of high immigration, the home affairs minister articulated why he believed the government can win the political argument against those competing to announce the lowest targeted Nom.
“The lower [Nom] levels will trash Australian services and trash the Australian economy,” he said.
Burke pointed out that denying skilled foreign workers the opportunity to bring in family members – as proposed by One Nation – would not free up more visas for more workers.
Instead, that approach would slash the number of foreign doctors, tradies, nurses and aged care workers willing to come to our country.

“The proportion of doctors who come to Australia with family attached to their application? 50%. How many construction workers come with family attached to their application? 50%. How many nurses and aged care workers come with family attached to their application? Two-thirds.”
Whether Burke and the Albanese government can convince the public its measured approach is enough is an open question.
“Let’s see if this lets out some of the hot air in the migration debate,” Gamlen said.

articles.title: Tony Burke rejects farmers’ claims that immigration changes will increase food prices
articles.summary:
Farming lobby says shoppers will see emptier shelves and higher prices because of restrictions on backpackers

  • Get our

blocks.text: The farming lobby’s claim that immigration rule changes will increase food prices for households is wrong, Tony Burke has said, describing moves to speed up processing of backpacker visas as a positive step for agriculture.

Burke unveiled Labor’s long-awaited reforms at the National Press Club on Thursday, flagging that the plan was more limited than the government would like, due to a lack of support for wider legislation from the Coalition.

But the package has received mixed reviews, with business groups and the Coalition saying it did not do enough to lower net overseas migration levels, while refugee advocates said it showed migrants remained “political punching bags”.

The National Farmers Federation’s chief executive, Mike Guerin, said farmers would see an immediate economic impact from restrictions on working holidaymakers and other temporary migrants. He warned producers were already struggling to get workers for the harvesting season.
Backpackers seeking to stay in Australia for more than a year will be subject to a new ballot, with places severely restricted for years two and three.
“We will see a lift in the price of food,” Guerin said.

“We will see emptier supermarkets ... And while it’s yet to play out directly for consumers, for people in the cities, it’s very close. We will not be able to finish the harvest this year, before Christmas.”
But Burke told Guardian Australia the plan was carefully formulated, reducing demand driven settings and giving the government great control, while not damaging the economy.
He said healthcare, construction and aged care all relied on overseas workers, and broader cuts would hurt essential services.
“The economic contribution matters in terms of services that people rely on.

“The announcement we made today is about getting the processing moving again for those backpacker visas that have an obligation, if you want the extra years, to work in the regions. That’s a significant advantage … the department getting moving on the processing of those again at a faster pace.”
Burke said the agriculture sector could utilise workers from the Pacific Australia labour mobility scheme, and producers had legal responsibilities to pay staff adequately.
“I don’t think consumers believe their pathway to paying less should rely on worker exploitation.”
after newsletter promotion

blocks.caption: Tony Burke says the changes are not like hardline immigration enforcement in other countries.  Photograph: Lukas Coch/AAP

blocks.text: The government’s changes include new compliance measures to deal with people overstaying their visa, but Burke said enforcement would be measured and sensible.
About 100 new additional compliance officers will be added, along with 250 additional beds in immigration detention.
Burke said the changes were not like hardline immigration enforcement in countries overseas, such as the approach used by Donald Trump’s administration.
But the Asylum Seeker Resource Centre said the planned increase in enforcement would leave Australia “smaller, meaner and more divided”.
“How much of its soul is the Labor party prepared to sacrifice chasing people who will never be satisfied,” founder Kon Karapanagiotidis said.
The Greens deputy leader, Mehreen Faruqi, criticised the increased immigration detention and bar on foreign students bringing family members to Australia.
“Labor’s move to force people to choose between their family and a chance to study in Australia is soulless mimicry of One Nation tactics,” Faruqi said.
“Pauline Hanson and her billionaire backers might as well be ghostwriting Labor’s immigration policy.”
Major employers welcomed the reforms, with the Minerals Council of Australia praising the government’s prioritisation of mining workers.

Big business lobby group the Australian Chamber of Commerce and Industry said the government had avoided a damaging overcorrection and the plan would help rebuild public confidence. But its chief executive, Andrew McKellar, warned its execution via ministerial directives meant policy was being held together by “the stroke of a pen”.
The Nationals leader, Matt Canavan, accused the government of using farmers and regional industries as “whipping boys for their failure to bring down migration”.
Cuts to the working holidaymaker program would lead to staff shortages, the Australian Restaurant and Cafe Association chief, Wes Lambert, warned.
“A chef, cook or hospitality manager filling a genuine shortage is valuable too,” Lambert said.
“Australia absolutely needs a sustainable migration system. But migration policy cannot simply be a numbers exercise. It must recognise where the workers are actually needed.”

articles.summary: A judge has denied Tamara Lich's request to travel internationally while she serves a house arrest sentence, including going on a Caribbean cruise and to visit the White House.

image.caption: Tamara Lich, one of the organizers of the 2022 convoy protest in Ottawa, leaves the courthouse for a lunch break in Ottawa on Thursday, April 3, 2025. (Spencer Colby/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Ottawa·Breaking
A judge has denied Tamara Lich's request to travel internationally while she serves a house arrest sentence, including going on a Caribbean cruise and to visit the White House.
Lich serving sentence for role in 2022 convoy protest
A judge has denied Tamara Lich's request to travel internationally while she serves a house arrest sentence, including going on a Caribbean cruise and to the White House.
Lich was found guilty in April 2025 of mischief and other offences for her role in organizing and sustaining the 2022 convoy protest that paralyzed downtown Ottawa for nearly a month.
She was handed a conditional sentence last October that included 12 months under house arrest.

A month after being sentenced, Lich asked for and received permission to leave her home in Medicine Hat, Alta., to attend her grandchildren’s school. Since then, she has travelled to other provinces for her job with Rebel News.
In July, Lich asked for permission to travel internationally.

She didn't offer the court a detailed itinerary, but her request mentions attending press events at the White House, going on a seven-day Caribbean cruise with Rebel News, and travelling to Arizona to speak with Rob Schneider, a right-wing comedian whose controversial content prompted his removal from a Saskatchewan stage in 2024.

Crown prosecutors said the additional exemptions would give her a "blank cheque" to travel internationally. They opposed the request, arguing that granting it was unnecessary and would diminish the impact of her sentence "to an unacceptable extent."
Her defence said in July she had "abided by the terms of her conditional sentence to the letter."

In Justice Heather Perkins McVey's ruling Thursday, she said there was not enough evidence to show Lich's request is needed, including to maintain employment, and it would go against the principle of her sentence.
More to come.

articles.title: As Charles refutes Earl Spencer’s claim about Diana, how royal statements give a glimpse behind palace doors
articles.summary:
From ‘there were three of us in this marriage’ to ‘recollections may vary’, a lot can be conveyed with a carefully worded phrase

As denials go,

blocks.text: As denials go, King Charles’s response to Earl Spencer’s allegations that Charles said after Diana’s death, “We’ll forget her soon enough”, was a masterclass in the diplomatic royal rebuke.
Rarely has Buckingham Palace responded to claims in countless books on royalty. But it was straight out of the block on this one.

Little over an hour after the Daily Mail, which is serialising Spencer’s memoir Swan Song about his sister, the late Diana, Princess of Wales, had published its first extract online, a statement was issued.
Charles, the headline claimed, had told Spencer days after Diana’s death and during a heated row over funeral arrangements: “Rest assured, we’ll forget her soon enough.”

The king’s swift countering, that “the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgment and colour memory in ways others do not recognise, even many years after such a loss”, will enter the canon of carefully constructed regal pushbacks.

blocks.caption: Charles’s swift rebuke suggests the palace acknowledged the damage Spencer’s claim could do and needed to set the record straight. Photograph: Toby Melville/Reuters

blocks.text: As rebukes go, it is up there with the late Queen Elizabeth II’s “some recollections may vary” in response to a torrent of allegations from the Duke and Duchess of Sussex in their Oprah Winfrey interview.

Senior courtiers are often drawn from the diplomatic service and thus highly-skilled in couching the passive-aggressive denial. Deploying delicate language to devastating effect is a stock in trade at the Foreign Office.
But it is a weapon to be used sparingly. The royal mantra is, usually, “never complain, never explain”.
However, Charles’s former communications secretary Julian Payne said: “This is a much more personal situation, given its author, and therefore has a greater ability to do harm.”

That is why the palace “felt the need to set the record straight and deny these remarks have been made”, Payne told the BBC’s Today programme. Given the amount of things the palace don’t comment on, “you can imagine the strength of feeling”, he added.

Payne remains close to the king and was due to be sitting alongside him at Thursday’s AI summit just hours later, so the fact he felt able to speak so freely suggests his robust defence of Charles came with official sanction.
What is said behind palace doors usually remains private. The language may be less sensitive. But a carefully chosen phrase in public pulls back the privacy screen.
When Diana, in her highly controversial Panorama interview, said “there were three of us in this marriage, so it was a bit crowded”, she reaped public revenge on her then husband and Camilla.

In return, Diana found herself on the sharp end of Elizabeth’s ire weeks later. After Diana failed to respond to the queen’s request that the couple divorce, a palace spokesperson issued a statement: “After considering the present situation, the queen wrote to both the prince and princess earlier this week and gave them her view, supported by the Duke of Edinburgh, that an early divorce is desirable.” The matter was now, officially, out of Diana’s hands.

blocks.caption: Harry and Meghan during their interview with Oprah in 2021, which led to the late queen’s ‘recollections may vary’ statement. Photograph: Reuters

blocks.text: White fury was behind the Duke and Duchess of Sussex’s statement in February 2021: “We can all live a life of service. Service is universal.” It was read as a succinct and direct challenge to the late queen’s insistence they could not keep their public service roles after stepping down as working royals.

Meghan was less direct in a 2019 interview with ITV’s Tom Bradby in which he asked her if she was OK juggling life as a royal with a newborn, Prince Archie. “Thank you for asking, because not many people have asked if I’m OK,” she replied. Was it directed at the palace and the institution? A huge number of the claims the Sussexes later made, in TV interviews and in Harry’s memoir Spare, were that the duchess had been unsupported throughout her time as a working royal.

One royal famously deficient in the art of the diplomatic royal rebuke, however, was the late Duke of Edinburgh. Philip was renowned for his gaffes. When a BBC journalist politely asked the queen at a banquet at the Élysée Palace if she was enjoying her stay in Paris in 2006, Philip dispensed with tact to snap: “Damn fool question!”

articles.title: Trump arch could have ‘adverse effects’ on nearby DC monuments, US park service says
articles.summary:
National Park Service lays out concerns that planned 250ft arch could interfere with historic sites in US capital

Donald Trump’s desired triumphal arch in downtown Washington DC will likely…

blocks.text: Donald Trump’s desired triumphal arch in downtown Washington DC will likely contribute “to adverse effects to historic properties”, according to the National Park Service’s planning document, but the construction is still planned to go forward.

The president’s 250ft arch could interfere with some of the most well-known views in the nation’s capital, including the symbolic relationship between Arlington House, the Arlington National Cemetery, the Arlington Memorial Bridge and the Lincoln Memorial, which face each other to represent the reunification of the United States after the civil war.
As a result, the arch’s construction could require supplemental planning and programming to preserve history, a document and emails obtained by the Washington Post on Wednesday outlined.
“Such adverse effects cannot be fully avoided while retaining the location-dependent purpose of the undertaking,” the National Park Service wrote in the document.

Despite concerns that the arch could interfere with historic sites and would require substantial construction management control, the Trump administration wants to move forward. The document was circulated among preservationists and other groups to review and sign by noon on Monday, according to an email obtained by the Washington Post.
The Guardian has asked the National Park Service for comment.
Historic preservationists, veterans and lawmakers have consistently raised concerns about the Trump administration building the massive triumphal arch in downtown DC.

Veterans filed a lawsuit in September, seeking to halt construction of the arch, believing it would harm the symbolic relationship of historic sites representing the reconciliation of war or disrupt burials at the Arlington National Cemetery.
Some lawmakers shared fears that the arch could further complicate DC’s airspace. But Trump has been emphatic about the arch, insisting it should be 250ft high to mark the US’s 250th anniversary.
Should construction of the arch move forward, the National Park Service outlined several ways it would mitigate disruptions and potential damage to nearby monuments.

That includes installing vibration plates near the Arlington Memorial Bridge and other sensitive sites to ensure construction remains within prescribed limits, enforcing limits on noise-generating activities, prohibiting unnecessary lighting, limiting work hours and more.
after newsletter promotion

The National Park Service’s document outlined roughly 37 nearby historic sites that could be affected, including the Lincoln Memorial, the National Mall, the Washington Monument, the Pentagon, the US Capitol and more.

But the National Park Service also outlined methods it could implement to preserve the history of the area, such as developing digital programs to explain the commemorative relationship between the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington House, to show before-and-after scenes of the skyline over the Potomac River, and to describe the significance of triumphal arches.
Local preservation officers could refuse to sign the agreement, which could trigger another process that involves the Advisory Council on Historic Preservation, a federal agency.

However, the Trump administration does not need the preservationists’ consent to move forward because it already received approval from the US Commission on Fine Arts, a federal advisory council made up of Trump appointees, and preliminary approval from the National Capital Planning Commission.

articles.title: Meta ordered to remove deepfakes as oversight board criticises ‘inadequate’ safeguards
articles.summary:
Facebook told it was wrong in leaving up AI-generated videos of a Labour councillor and Muslim campaigner, amid calls to curb fakes

Meta’s “supreme court” has ordered the tech company to…

blocks.text: Meta’s “supreme court” has ordered the tech company to take down deepfake videos of a UK politician and a young Muslim woman from Facebook and do more to tackle AI-generated fake imagery.

A fake video showing a Labour party councillor in Scotland making inflammatory comments about refugees should not have been left up by Facebook, the board said. It also ruled that an AI-generated video of a Muslim campaign volunteer should have been removed after it falsely depicted her offering health advice while carrying out absurd exercises or eating junk food.
The board said Meta’s safeguards are “consistently and fundamentally inadequate” to address the rapid rise of AI deepfakes.

“From politicians to private citizens, AI-generated deepfakes are increasingly being used to harass and silence women from engaging in public discourse,” said Pamela San Martin, an oversight board co-chair.

“These cases demonstrate a broader, troubling pattern in which women who engage publicly on issues are disproportionately subjected to harassment and misinformation. Meta and other social media platforms need more robust policies to address the proliferation of deepfakes.”
In the Scotland clip, the councillor is falsely represented as saying: “Refugees are welcome here, even if they rape our women, because white people do that too.”

The oversight board, a quasi-independent body whose decisions are binding, said the video of the councillor appeared to be AI-generated, as indicated by the audio not being fully synchronised to the unnamed councillor’s facial movements.
Even when raised directly with the company by the board, Meta decided the video did not violate its content policies and did not merit an AI label.

In a blogpost published on Thursday, the board said the post should have been removed because it violated Meta’s rules on hateful conduct by alleging criminal and predatory sexual behaviour by refugees as an entire group and not as individuals. The video should also have received a “high risk AI” label, said the board, as it called for tougher measures on deepfakes.

“The majority [of the board] finds that Meta needs more robust policies on deepfakes, including expanding the situations when ‘high risk’ labels can be applied, more measures to reduce the spread of deceptive AI content, increasing the penalties for accounts that repeatedly share it, and more transparency on data around when AI labels are applied,” it said.

The board recommended nine policy changes at Meta, including ensuring algorithms demote content labelled “high risk”, making such posts less likely to appear in users’ feeds. It also recommended that Meta makes it more difficult for users to view AI-generated content by, for instance, introducing a warning screen that requires a click-through before viewing the content.

In a separate ruling, the board also ordered Meta to take down from Facebook an AI-generated video mocking a young Muslim woman in Europe taking part in a campaign to improve menstrual health education and reduce stigma around health conditions for women and girls from ethnic minority backgrounds. AI-manipulated videos and images mocking the woman had tens of millions of views online, including on Meta platforms.

The board singled out one of the videos – showing the woman exercising absurdly and eating junk food – as a breach of the company’s bullying and harassment policy. It recommended the post be removed and made three policy recommendations, including changing its definition of “unwanted manipulated imagery” to cover deepfakes of a private individual saying or doing things they did not say or do.
The board was set up by Meta in 2020 to serve as a referee for content on its platforms. Meta has been approached for comment.

articles.title: Missing sabungeros case continues with only one complainant attending
articles.summary: There is one complainant left who continues to attend the hearings in the case of the missing sabungeros (cockfighting enthusiasts) after other families were allegedly paid off.

blocks.text: Published September 17, 2026 10:36pm
There is one complainant left who continues to attend the hearings in the case of the missing sabungeros (cockfighting enthusiasts) after other families were allegedly paid off.

In a "24 Oras" report from Emil Sumangil on Thursday, Charlene Lasco, the sister of the missing master agent Ricardo “Jonjon” Lasco Jr., is the lone attendee at the Quezon City Regional Trial Court where the case of the missing sabungeros is being heard.
Jonjon Lasco was seen on CCTV footage being abducted in San Pablo, Laguna in August 2021.
Whistleblower Julie "Dondon" Patidongan admitted to being the one who paid P2 million to a group to kidnap Jonjon Lasco.
Now, Charlene Lasco said that she could no longer contact her colleagues who vowed to seek justice for their missing loved ones.

“Gusto ko lang kung magsabi sa mga kasamahan namin na, nakakalungkot na umalis kayo… akala ko tuloy-tuloy yung paglaban namin, pagkuha namin ng hustisya pero wala eh, talagang... siyempre, talagang kailangan naman nila ng pera,” Charlene Lasco said.
(I just want to say to our colleagues that it is sad that you left… I thought that the fight would continue, that we will try to get justice but of course… they really need the money.)

Charlene Lasco said she heard rumors that the other families of the missing sabungeros were paid off, with some of them directly telling her. Charlene Lasco herself has received offers to abandon the case, but said that it was not money that she needed, but justice.
“Yung aming mga kasamahan, ito ang sinasabi, na kapag na-areglo na sila, susuko si Mr. Atong Ang, magpapakulong ng sandali, pagkatapos, lalabas, magbi-bail, tapos na ang kaso,” Charlene Lasco said.

(Some of our colleagues, this is what they said, that once they reach an arrangement. Mr. Atong Ang will surrender, he will be imprisoned for a bit, and then after, he will get out after posting bail and then the case is done.)

A few sources from law enforcement agencies told GMA News that there is news that Ang’s camp is trying to connect with them to surrender. However the Philippine National Police (PNP) said that they have not received any word from Ang.

"The PNP has not received any formal communication or feelers of surrender from Atong Ang or his representatives. Beyond that, operational matters of this nature are not something we can discuss publicly, as doing so may compromise ongoing efforts to serve the warrant of arrest,” PNP spokesperson Police Colonel Allen Rae Co said.
Charlene Lasco said she hoped that the government’s case would still stand because of Patidongan.

“Sana yung gobyerno, makuha ang puno’t dulo kung bakit nawawala yung mga complainant,” Charlene Lasco said. (I hope that the government will get to the source of why the complainants are disappearing.) —Jean Mangaluz/LDF, GMA News

articles.title: Germany cuts development aid despite growing crises
articles.summary: The budget of Germany's Federal Ministry for Economic Cooperation and Development (BMZ) is set to shrink for the fifth consecutive year. Aid organizations warn that the cuts could have dramatic…

image.caption: NGOs took to the street outside the chancellery to demonstrate against cutting development aidImage: Giulia Saudelli/DW

blocks.text: Germany's Development Minister, Reem Alabali Radovan, opened her latest speech in the lower house of parliament, the Bundestag, with a litany of catastrophes and suffering: floods in Nepal, heat waves, forests engulfed in flames, rivers running dry, and crop failures caused by drought and lack of rainfall.

"Millions of people are facing hunger," said the minister from the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD). "And one thing is clear: the climate crisis is threatening the entire world. No country can tackle it alone."

Radovan opened the debate on the federal government's proposed 2027 budget for her ministry with a stark assessment. The budget is set to shrink for the fifth consecutive year, falling from just over €10 billion to just under €9.5 billion. In 2022, it still stood at nearly €14 billion. Since then, the ministry's budget has been reduced by roughly one third.
Fighting to end suffering in Africa's conflict zones

How does this sharp decline square with the dramatic picture painted by Germany's development minister herself? She points to the new strategy she unveiled in January, when she declared: "Development policy will become an even more important pillar of German security, alongside diplomacy and defense."
Funding for humanitarian aid stagnates

Aid organizations reacted skeptically to this policy shift when it was first announced, and their concerns have deepened in light of the latest funding cuts. "The renewed reductions in funding for international cooperation are further exacerbating an already critical situation," said Michael Herbst of VENRO, the umbrella organization representing around 150 development and humanitarian NGOs.

Herbst also criticizes the stagnant budget for humanitarian aid administered by the German Foreign Office. While it exceeded €3 billion in 2022, it has remained at just €1 billion since 2025. In light of worsening global crises, VENRO is calling for a change of course. "Next year, we will need to invest more in combating hunger because the conflict involving Iran and the dry summer are expected to trigger a sharp decline in agricultural yields," Herbst said, explaining the organization's demand for substantially higher funding.
Ten million people left without assistance

The impact of the cuts is already clearly visible, the umbrella organization stresses, citing a survey of its member organizations. The number of funded projects is declining significantly. "Our sample of 34 organizations shows that, among these organizations alone, more than ten million fewer people are being reached with assistance."

"And many local partner organizations, which are indispensable to effective development cooperation and humanitarian assistance, are no longer able to operate," Herbst added. He also stressed that the full impact of these far-reaching cuts is unlikely to become apparent for another three to four years.
Should the development budget be exempt from Germany's 'debt brake'?

The federal government's belt-tightening across virtually all ministries is a consequence of the Zeitenwende announced by then-Chancellor Olaf Scholz(SPD) in response to Russia's invasion of Ukraine. Since then, Germany has embarked on a major military buildup, increasing its defense budget year after year, while nearly all other ministries have had to make do with significantly less funding.

Herbst, a member of VENRO's executive board, is calling on the German Bundestag to exempt both development cooperation and humanitarian assistance from the country's so-called 'debt brake'. "After all, exceptions have already been made for the modernization of the Bundeswehr and for military aid to Ukraine," he points out. Herbst hopes that such a move would enable Germany to once again assume greater responsibility on the international stage.
Germany's Radovan warns SDGs unlikely to be met by 2030
Less money, less impact?

Jamila Schäfer, a member of parliament from the opposition Green Party, made a similar argument during the Bundestag debate on the development ministry's budget. Climate action and development cooperation, she argued, are not acts of charity but are firmly in Germany's own interest.

"Germany must invest in its defense capabilities, but security is not created through investments in the defense budget alone," Schäfer argued. "Those who strengthen military security while cutting support for international stability have a blind spot in their security policy."

Nicolas Zippelius, a lawmaker from the governing centre-right conservative alliance, the Christian Democratic Union and Christian Social Union (CDU/CSU), sees the ongoing cuts to development spending differently. In his view, every ministry must contribute to consolidating the federal budget. "Less money does not necessarily mean a smaller impact. Instead, it should encourage us to focus more clearly on priorities and critically review existing structures."

Zippelius dismisses demands to exempt the development ministry from Germany's 'debt brake'. "The key question is whether every euro spent is directed to where it can make the greatest difference." The Christian Democrat argues that success in development cooperation, as in other areas of policy, should be judged not by the size of the budget but by the impact it achieves.
German Development Minister Reem Alabali Radovan in Kenya
The case for more prevention

Jan Sebastian Friedrich-Rust, who heads the humanitarian and development aid organizationAction Against Hunger, has a very different view. "The cuts planned for the 2027 budget are short-sighted and dangerous. As a result, up to 22.6 million people worldwide could die by 2030," he said in a written statement to DW.

Cuts to development cooperation and humanitarian aid are also fiscally short-sighted, Friedrich-Rust argues. "Hunger, crises and instability generate long-term costs that far exceed the cost of prevention. Those who cut spending today are merely postponing the bill and ultimately making it much more expensive," he warned.

To underscore its concerns, the alliance Action Against Hunger delivered a petition to the leaders of the governing coalition of SPD and CDU/CSU parliamentary groups on the eve of the Bundestag's budget debate. The appeal, titled "Don't Balance the Budget at the Expense of Solidarity: Strengthen International Aid!", garnered around 100,000 signatures.
This article was translated from German.

articles.title: Macalintal to Marcos: Veto bill postponing BSKE
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — Election lawyer Romulo Macalintal on Thursday urged President Marcos to veto the measure postponing the Nov. 2 Barangay and Sangguniang Kabataan Elections (BSKE), adding he…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — Election lawyer Romulo Macalintal on Thursday urged President Marcos to veto the measure postponing the Nov. 2 Barangay and Sangguniang Kabataan Elections (BSKE), adding he wants to be personally heard by Marcos regarding the matter.

The House of Representatives adopted the Senate’s version of a bill extending the term of village and youth councilors to five years on Wednesday, sending the measure that effectively postpones their elections straight to Malacañang for executive action.
But in a letter transmitted and received by the Office of the President today, Macalintal decried that signing or allowing the measure to lapse into law “will inflict severe constitutional injury.”
“In light of the foregoing, may I respectfully request an opportunity to be personally heard by Your Excellency on this matter?” Macalintal said in the letter.

“Furthermore, in the highest interest of protecting the Philippine Constitution, upholding the rule of law, and preserving the sanctity of the ballot, I most respectfully implore Your Excellency to exercise your constitutional prerogative by vetoing the subject enrolled bill,” he continued.
According to him, the bill is a direct violation of the electorate’s right of suffrage and lacks complete substantive justification and operational readiness.

Macalintal said, “If the legislative objective is truly to adjust future terms of office, any new term structure should have been applied strictly and prospectively to the officials winning the upcoming November 2, 2026 election.”
“That less restrictive path would have fulfilled term-setting goals without trampling upon the electorate’s fundamental right to choose their grassroots leaders,” he also said.
Macalintal was one of the petitioners in the consolidated petitions earlier granted by the SC that declared the postponement of the 2022 BSKE as “unconstitutional.”
The Commission on Elections said unless a law is passed before the end of September, the filing of certificates of candidacy scheduled from Sept. 28 to Oct. 5 will push through. /cb

articles.summary: Manitobans no longer need to remember to spring forward or fall back one hour on their clocks.

image.caption: Manitoba joins several other provinces and territories that have adopted or are moving toward a permanent time, including British Columbia, Yukon, Northwest Territories, Alberta and Saskatchewan. (Elise Amendola/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: Manitoba
Manitobans no longer need to remember to spring forward or fall back one hour on their clocks.
Next scheduled time change was to take place Nov. 1
Daylight time will be in place permanently, Premier Wab Kinew announced in a news release Thursday.
This change means clocks will not revert to standard time on Nov. 1.
Manitoba joins several other provinces and territories that have adopted or are moving toward a permanent time, including British Columbia, Yukon, Northwest Territories, Alberta and Saskatchewan.
Just six months ago, Kinew said his government was too busy with more important matters to consider changes to the clocks.
He was asked about it in early March, shortly after B.C. announced it intended to remain on daylight time permanently.

items: Days of time change 'pretty much at the end' in Manitoba, premier suggests
Time for a survey: Province asks public to weigh in on future of time change in Manitoba

blocks.text: He later softened his stance, suggesting it may be time to revisit the issue.

Then in May, the province launched a survey, asking the public to weigh in the issue. For those who did want to see the twice-annual changes halted, the survey asked if they preferred to stay on standard or daylight time.

In its news release at the time the survey launched, the province included a link to an analysis by Manitoba Health, which concluded that eliminating the time change would be better for population health.

On Thursday, the province said nearly 72,000 votes were submitted in its survey and 92 per cent of respondents wanted to see an end to seasonal time changes, with 58 per cent preferring permanent daylight time and 34 per cent siding with standard time.

Permanent daylight time is good for health, business and families with young kids, whose routines, especially sleep cycles, can be disrupted for days with those one-hour time changes, Kinew said in the news release on Thursday.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Darren Bernhardt has been with CBC Manitoba since 2009 and specializes in offbeat and local history stories. He is the author of two bestselling books: The Lesser Known: A History of Oddities from the Heart of the Continent, and Prairie Oddities: Punkinhead, Peculiar Gravity and More Lesser Known Histories.

articles.title: Australian athlete apologizes for racing with diarrhea, forfeits the Beijing competition she won
articles.summary: Australian Joanna Wietrzyk, who started a global uproar after soiling herself and leaking feces at the popular indoor fitness competition, has apologized for continuing to race and forfeited her win.

image.caption: Joanna Wietrzyk of Australia takes part in the Hyrox Beijing 2026 competition at the National Speed Skating Oval on Saturday in Beijing. She issued an apology on Thursday for continuing to race with diarrhea. (Fred Lee/Getty Images)

blocks.text: World·New
Australian Joanna Wietrzyk, who started a global uproar after soiling herself and leaking feces at the popular indoor fitness competition, has apologized for continuing to race and forfeited her win.
Hyrox updates its competition rules after Joanna Wietrzyk left feces on shared equipment
The Hyrox athlete who started a global uproar after soiling herself and leaking feces at the popular indoor fitness competition has apologized for continuing to race, and forfeited her win.

"I want to offer my sincere apology to the people of China, my fellow competitors, the spectators and the Hyrox organizers for what happened during the race in Beijing," Australian Joanna Wietrzyk wrote in a statement posted to Instagram Thursday morning.
"Looking back, I regret the decision to not have stepped off the track. I recognize that I should have made a different choice."

Wietrzyk explained she felt "completely fit and healthy at the start of the race, with no reason to expect any illness." She added that, "on reflection," she decided to retroactively forfeit her win and the points she earned.
"I know my actions had an impact beyond myself, and I am genuinely sorry to everyone who was affected."

The graphic images of world record holder Wietrzyk competing with feces running down her legs at Saturday's Hyrox in Beijing have sparked debate about the health and safety of competitors versus the mentality that a win is a win, no matter the cost.

Footage showed Wietrzyk continue to push through her events using communal equipment such as ropes, sandbags, rowing machines and medicine balls, and doing burpees and lunges on a shared indoor track. She was the pro women's champion with a time of 1:01:23.

"Go hard or go home … a win is a win," Wietrzyk posted — then later deleted — on Instagram after the event along with a selfie in what appeared to be a hospital bed, according to multiple news outlets.
Hyrox refunding affected participants

As the incident went viral, online commenters were quick to point out the health risks for other competitors, with many people saying Wietrzyk should have quit or Hyrox should have disqualified her. Others are calling on Hyrox to refund the other competitors or offer them compensation.

On Wednesday, Hyrox China announced it was refunding the entry costs to more than 1,000 participants affected by the incident, according to the South China Morning Post. A spectator at the event told the outlet that feces was visible on the track about 30 minutes after Wietrzyk started her race, causing several runners to slip.
Other athletes who competed in the same race described having to use equipment smeared with feces.

items: Hyrox athlete won competition while leaking diarrhea. Was she right to push through?
'Extreme' workouts drive spike in 'rhabdo' cases among young N.L. women, says doctor

blocks.text: On Monday, Hyrox co-founder Moritz Fürste wrote in an Instagram statement that the organization has since changed its rules to prevent similar situations from happening again.

Its official rulebook already lists penalties for other bodily fluids, noting that spitting or clearing of nostrils onto the floor is strictly prohibited. Until this week, there was no mention of penalties for feces contaminating the race course.

"I am learning from this experience and will carry those lessons with me, including remembering that there is more to life than racing and knowing when it is right to step away," Wietrzyk wrote in her apology.
She added that she will be taking some time to "recover, reflect and look after myself and my family away from the noise."

articles.title: Nicholas Brandram’s family deny he was ‘Putney pusher’ and say Met police pressure led to his death
articles.summary:
Banker, 44, was arrested in connection with 2017 incident but family say ‘no credible evidence’ he was involved

The family of Nicholas Brandram have denied he was the so-called “Putney…

blocks.text: The family of Nicholas Brandram have denied he was the so-called “Putney pusher” and said he “took his own life after months of immense pressure caused by a Metropolitan police investigation”.
Brandram, 44, was found unresponsive at a property in Chiswick, west London, believed to be his home, on Tuesday evening.
The senior city banker had been arrested in June in connection with an incident nearly 10 years ago on Putney Bridge, in which a jogger shoved a woman headfirst into the path of an oncoming bus.
The Metropolitan police said Brandram had been released under investigation after his arrest.
On Thursday, a spokesperson for the police complaints watchdog, the Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC), confirmed the force had referred itself over its prior contact with Brandram.

He said: “We have received a mandatory referral from the Met police relating to prior contact officers had with Nicholas Brandram, who was sadly found unresponsive and declared deceased on 15 September. We are currently assessing the referral before deciding whether further action is required from us.”

Earlier, a statement released on behalf of his immediate family on Thursday said Brandram had taken his own life after “months of immense pressure caused by a Metropolitan police investigation into whether he was the so-called ‘Putney Pusher’”.
His family denied his involvement in the incident and claimed the police had no forensic evidence linking him to it.

They said: “There was no forensic evidence linking Nick to it, no evidence placing him on Putney Bridge at that time, and no credible evidence that he was the man shown in the footage. In fact, the evidence proved the opposite.

“Despite that, the police chose to arrest Nick rather than invite him to attend for interview. They searched his home, and the Met police press team then released information which inevitably led to speculation and Nick being identified in subsequent reporting.”

The family added: “For Nick, the consequences did not disappear. He was left for months carrying the stigma of an appalling allegation which the police themselves clearly recognised was unsupported by the evidence.
“He lived with the shame, anxiety, humiliation, and extraordinary pressure created by a wholly unnecessary investigation.”

They said the police had repeatedly been asked to end their investigation and had been warned about the impact the investigation was having on Brandram’s mental health, saying: “Even then, the investigation was not brought to an end. As a result, Nick is dead.”
The Met has been approached for comment.
Brandram was a director at HSBC and had previously served in the military, reaching the rank of captain.

He was the grandson of Princess Katherine of Greece, who was the great-granddaughter of Queen Victoria, the Daily Telegraph reported in 2013, when he was convicted of crashing his Harley-Davidson motorbike into a female cyclist around Hyde Park Corner and driving off without leaving his details.
In an interview with the Citywealth website in March this year, Brandram said he was a senior relationship manager at HSBC Private Bank.

He said: “I usually bicycle into our office in Mayfair from my home in west London. And then from there, can either stay at my desk, go to Canary Wharf or the City, or get on a train or go to the airport. My first meeting is ideally over breakfast and I’m ideally home for bath time. I’m a co-parenting single father with a three-year-old.”

Brandram said his proudest professional achievement was being invited to a Buckingham Palace garden party after military service in Afghanistan, and that the person he most admired was his mother. “She raised three children as a single parent and is the busiest person I know,” he said. “I’ve never met someone with greater moral integrity and courage, as well as resilience and stamina.”

articles.title: Baby found under floor in 19th-century house was killed with twine, UK inquest concludes
articles.summary:
‘Terrible thing’ happened to infant boy found wrapped in 1910 newspaper at Bishop Auckland property, says coroner

A baby boy who was found with twine looped and knotted round his neck and…
articles.byline: Mark Brown North of England correspondent

blocks.text: A baby boy who was found with twine looped and knotted round his neck and wrapped in a 116-year-old newspaper was unlawfully killed, a coroner has concluded
Crispin Oliver on Thursday said the child, known only as Baby Auckland, had been garrotted by an unknown person.
He said it was an “unusual case, legally and evidentially”. The whole story, he added, was “very sad and singular”.

Oliver said: “Clearly, this was a terrible thing that happened to a defenceless infant. It happened in our community. But it happened over a century ago, and it is heartwarming how the public and individuals in this community have stepped up to do the right thing by Baby Auckland.”
The inquest heard that the skeletal remains of the baby had been found during renovations on the second floor of a late 19th-century house in Bishop Auckland, County Durham, on 29 July 2024.

They were found by the house owner, Peter Moody, while he was laying a new floor. In a statement he said he had made the discovery when he lifted up a floorboard. He contacted the county council, unsure of whether he needed to call the police.
DCI Mel Sutherland told the inquest he had been on duty in Bishop Auckland when he was alerted to the discovery of skeletal remains in a town centre house.

After they were confirmed as human, he supervised the sealing of the house to keep it forensically sterile, while a forensic anthropologist was contacted. That scientist, Dr Micol Zuppello, travelled up that evening and spent two days at the house investigating.

The baby’s skeleton was mostly complete, the inquest in Crook heard, bar a missing toe tip. The remains were partly mummified. Carbon dating could conclusively establish only that the baby died between the 17th century and 1955.
A postmortem of the skeleton was carried out by Zupello and Dr Louise Mulcahy, a Home Office pathologist for north-east England based at the Royal Victoria Infirmary in Newcastle.

Mulcahy said the baby had been 38-40 weeks, with no signs of traumatic injury, and had twine looped around his neck. She said it had been looped around the neck three times, knotted, and then looped again.

blocks.caption: PCSOs and a forensics officer outside the building in Bishop Auckland in 2024, after the discovery was made. Photograph: Owen Humphreys/PA

blocks.text: It was not possible to say, she added, if it had been tight or loose. The medical cause of death, she said, was “unascertained”.

The skeleton was too old to be able to confirm or refute the presence of natural disease, she said. In the absence of soft tissue it was not possible, the inquest heard, to say if there had been any assault or trauma. Equally, it was not possible to say with any certainty if the baby had been stillborn or not.
Oliver said police had “had to think laterally” during their investigation. He praised Sutherland for “leaving no stone unturned”.
Sutherland described some of the techniques they had used to investigate further, including DNA testing. All were inconclusive.
He said the newspaper was very brown, but articles could be seen. It was called The Umpire and dated June 1910.
Sutherland said that in 1911 census data, the building was described as dining rooms, meaning “a cafe-type establishment”.

A public appeal was made for people who thought they might be related to come forward. Two sisters came forward who believed they were related to a servant at the house, but DNA testing revealed no match.
During the whole investigation, Sutherland said, there had been “very little to go on”.

Oliver asked if the twine might have been used for a religious artefact, but nothing like that had been found, Sutherland said. There was also no evidence to suggest any link to midwifery practices of the time.
A knot specialist could not be used, the inquest heard, because the nearest person was in the Netherlands and would have been too expensive for this type of investigation.
Baby Auckland was laid to rest at Bishop Auckland cemetery in April this year, with professionals involved giving their services for free.
Sutherland said it had been two years of investigating, “challenging and frustrating at times, but heartwarming to see the send-off he got at the end”.
