articles.title: FBI warned ICE agents could be targeted by fake ‘tradwife’ dating profiles, memo reveals
articles.summary:
Exclusive: Internal FBI memo, reviewed by the Guardian, said women wanted to dox and ‘embarrass’ agents, but provided few details

The FBI internally warned that a group of women were…

blocks.text: The FBI internally warned that a group of women were creating fake online dating accounts with “tradwife” aesthetics in an effort to lure US immigration agents and “dox” them.

The FBI in Chicago disseminated a brief memo to other law enforcement officials across the US on the potential threat to agents in February, warning that “as of late January 2026, a small group of women allegedly were creating fictitious online dating profiles with the purpose of attracting and then doxxing law enforcement participating in immigration enforcement”. The report, which was shared with the Guardian, provided few details about the alleged scheme and did not explain the source of the information.

“These profiles were incorporating imagery of a ‘traditional wife’ aesthetic and listing specific interests in an attempt to appeal to … individuals in law enforcement,” the FBI continued. “The objective was to lure affiliated law enforcement personnel into an online or in-person interaction under the guise of a date, after which the individuals would be publicly exposed and doxed online. The tactic is intended to generate public embarrassment and deter immigration enforcement activity.”

Property of the People, a government-transparency non-profit, obtained the document through a public records request, one of many internal records the group has collected revealing internal law enforcement concerns about activists organizing against Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).

The FBI’s “situational information report” did not list the dating sites allegedly used by the women or where they were located, nor did it specify whether agents had actually been exposed. The memo aimed “to raise awareness” about this doxing “technique”, the FBI wrote, adding a disclaimer that the report was “not finally evaluated intelligence”.

The FBI’s “tradwife” comments were a reference to the trend popularized in recent years by influencers promoting traditional gender roles, with women romanticizing domesticity. “Doxing” generally refers to publishing someone’s private information online without their consent, though the administration has used the term loosely, claiming doxing includes posting videos of officers.

The FBI declined to answer detailed questions about the memo, saying the bureau doesn’t generally comment on intelligence briefings. A spokesperson added in an email: “The FBI regularly shares information with our law enforcement partners to assist in protecting the communities they serve as well as protecting those who serve and protect communities. The FBI is committed to ensuring that law enforcement officers are safe from threats or violence while performing their duties.”
The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) did not respond to requests for comment.

The memo was sent weeks after the New York Post, a conservative outlet, ran a story saying that “lefty TikTokkers” were “orchestrating groups of women” to “chase dick picks and selfies of ICE agents in a twisted scheme to dox them”. That story cited Libs of TikTok, a rightwing account that had posted a screenshot of someone claiming to be part of a Facebook group dedicated to going on dates with agents to expose them. The article listed a handful of posts and videos from users discussing this tactic, though it did not include interviews with anyone who claimed to be duping agents and there was no evidence agents had been tricked.
The news coverage did not mention women using “tradwife” imagery, so it’s unclear whether the FBI may have received direct accounts from targeted agents or was simply summarizing social media trends.

“It’s absurd the FBI issued a thinly-sourced security alert about ICE agents’ online dating troubles,” Ryan Shapiro, executive director of Property of the People, said in a statement. “It’s equally ludicrous the FBI is spending taxpayer dollars to protect ICE agents from possible ‘embarrassment’ at the hands of a supposed ‘small group of women’ who might name and ridicule them online.”

Mike German, a former FBI agent and longtime civil liberties advocate, reviewed the document for the Guardian and said it was odd the briefing did not have footnotes or citations. The briefing said the intelligence came from a “collaborative source”.

“The rightwing echo chamber creates threats and the government’s intelligence apparatus just repeats those threats without any context, more detail or any instruction of how agents or officers should respond,” said German, arguing it seemed likely the briefing was inspired by the New York Post story. “They must have run out of other threats.”
The document, German added, “reinforces the paranoid ‘us versus them’ mentality within law enforcement”.

The briefing comes as US law enforcement has raised increasing alarms about officials, and ICE agents in particular, being “doxed”. More than a dozen internal law enforcement reports, obtained via records requests by Property of the People, include similar warnings about doxing.

An October 2025 report from the US army said there was “credible intelligence” that “cartels” had offered to pay gang members and others in the US to dox, assault or kidnap immigration officers. That report cited charges against a man accused of a murder-for-hire plot targeting a top border patrol leader, but the man was found not guilty months later.

In a November 2025 report, the FBI warned that AI, facial-recognition and automated data-scraping tools had “increased the scale and accuracy of doxxing attacks” targeting ICE officers. The alert said people had published ICE officers’ names, photos, license plates, locations and family details, citing various crowdsourced efforts by activists to report ICE sightings.

In a January 2026 New York police department “terrorism brief”, the NYPD warned of “violent rhetoric” and “extremist messaging” on social media after the killing of Renee Good, including “calls to ‘hunt down’, ‘dox’, and kill ICE personnel”. The report cited a small number of online posts that appeared to call for violence.

And a May 2026 alert from Customs and Border Protection (CBP), a branch of DHS, warned that smart glasses, which have cameras, could be used to surveil, record and potentially dox CBP personnel. A CBP spokesperson did not comment directly on the document, but said in an email that smart glasses “pose unique security and intelligence risks because of their ability to discreetly capture audio and video” and the agency continues to monitor technology trends. Property of the People shared records with the Guardian earlier this month showing law enforcement across the US have grown increasingly concerned that smart glasses could be used against officers.

Other law enforcement agencies that have raised concerns about ICE agents being doxed in internal records include the FBI in Los Angeles, the Amtrak police department, an Idaho law enforcement consortium, a Florida fusion center of local and federal agencies, and the Federal Protective Service, which is also part of DHS.

There can be safety concerns if agents’ home addresses or family information is exposed, and two activists were convicted of “stalking” in California after prosecutors said they followed an agent home and publicly disclosed the location.

But German argued law enforcement’s claims about doxing were misguided, noting that ICE officers are domestic servants, not “secret agents” whose identities must be shielded: “These are agents working on the public dime. The public has a right to know who they are and what their qualifications and training are.”

articles.title: Buckingham Palace hits back at claims in a book by Princess Diana’s brother
articles.summary: Buckingham Palace has forcefully denied a claim by the brother of the late Princess Diana that King Charles said she would soon be forgotten after her death.

image.caption: King Charles gestures at The King's Foundation's Harmony in Food and Farming Summit, at the foundation's headquarters in Cumnock, Scotland, on Wednesday. (Jonathan Brady/Pool PA/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: World·New
Buckingham Palace has forcefully denied a claim by the brother of the late Princess Diana that King Charles said she would soon be forgotten after her death.
Earl Spencer recounts traumatic days after Diana was killed in a Paris car crash in 1997

In a new book, Charles Spencer recounts the traumatic days after Diana was killed in a car crash in Paris in 1997 at the age of 36. He alleges that he argued with the then-Prince Charles, Diana’s estranged husband, over palace plans for Prince William and Prince Harry to walk behind her coffin during the funeral procession.

Spencer says he told Charles that Diana would not have wanted her sons, then 15 and 12, to undergo the ordeal. He claims Charles told him: "rest assured, we'll forget her soon enough." He accuses Charles of having "contempt" for his ex-wife.

items: Expert investigation reveals truth about Princess Diana's death more than 25 years ago

blocks.text: The Daily Mail is publishing extracts from Spencer's book, Swan Song: Diana, My Sister, which is due to be published next week.
Buckingham Palace responded late Wednesday with an extremely strong statement by the measured standards of the royal household.

"While we do not comment on books as a matter of principle, His Majesty is mindful that the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgment and colour memory in ways others do not recognize, even many years after such a loss," it said.
Tensions between the palace and Diana's aristocratic Spencer relatives after her death have been much discussed and were dramatized in the film The Queen and the TV series The Crown.

Many felt the palace was slow to acknowledge the global outpouring of grief over Diana's death, which forced the royals to recognize that her common touch had allowed her to connect with people in ways that eluded the rest of the Royal Family. The more emotionally literate approach of Prince William and Prince Harry — and, in recent years, the King — is a legacy of that time.
Prince Charles, then 32, married 20-year-old Lady Diana Spencer in a lavish ceremony at St. Paul's Cathedral in 1981. The couple separated in 1992 and divorced in 1996.

items: Charles confirms Harry and Meghan to remain non-working royals after their return to U.K.

blocks.text: Diana's younger brother, Charles Spencer — the 9th Earl Spencer — has long clashed with the Royal Family over their treatment of his sister.

In a searing eulogy at Diana's funeral, Spencer vowed that Diana's "blood family" would carry on her "imaginative and loving" legacy in raising her two sons. The speech was widely considered a swipe at the Royal Family.

articles.title: IS member sentenced to 20 years in prison for role in 2021 Kabul airport bombing
articles.summary:
Mohammad Sharifullah, 28, was convicted of aiding the terrorist group that took credit for the suicide bombing

An Islamic State group member was sentenced Wednesday to 20 years in prison…

blocks.text: An Islamic State group member was sentenced Wednesday to 20 years in prison for aiding the terrorist organization that took credit for a suicide bombing that killed 13 US service members and about 160 Afghans at the Kabul airport five years ago during the US military’s chaotic withdrawal from the country.

A federal jury in Virginia had convicted Mohammad Sharifullah in April of providing material support to the IS affiliate known as Islamic State Khorasan Province (ISKP). But jurors could not agree whether he bore some responsibility for the airport bombing on 26 August 2021.

US troops were conducting an evacuation operation at the airport when a suicide bomber detonated an improvised explosive device near an entry point known as Abbey Gate. Sharifullah’s role in the attack was scouting a route to Hamid Karzai international airport, prosecutors said.
Sharifullah, 28, received the maximum sentence for his one-count conviction in an international terrorism case that Donald Trump heralded last year during a speech to a joint session of Congress.

Sharifullah did not testify at his trial and declined to address the court before US district judge Anthony Trenga imposed the sentence. The judge said the defendant was a “dedicated terrorist” who expressed no remorse for the “unfathomable” grief and suffering that he had caused.

Trenga heard victim impact statements from several parents of the US service members. From a podium only a few feet from where Sharifullah sat, they took turns paying tribute to their children’s sacrifices and describing how the attack has shattered their families.
Mark Schmitz of Missouri asked Sharifullah to turn and look at him as he spoke about the life and death of his 20-year-old son, Marine Corps Lance Cpl Jared Schmitz.
“They may have taken his life, but they’ll never take his legacy,” Mark Schmitz said. “A bomb killed my son. It did not kill what he stood for.”
Paula Knauss-Selph, whose son, Army Staff Sgt Ryan Knauss, was killed in the Abbey Gate bombing, said the family was “forever changed” by the attack.
“No justice will ever be enough to mend my broken heart,” she said.

Sharifullah requested a 17-year prison sentence, while prosecutors sought 20 years. His lawyers said he was never an ISKP leader and had not been convicted of any conduct related to the airport suicide bombing.
“He was brought here because the government believed he participated in the Abbey Gate attack, a theory which it was unable to prove at trial,” defense attorneys wrote.
Prosecutors said in their sentencing memo that “from his teenage years, when he pledged an oath of allegiance to [ISKP], Sharifullah’s carnage was driven by hate. Hate towards Americans.”

Jurors convicted Sharifullah of providing material support to ISKP. They deadlocked on whether any deaths at the airport “resulted from” that conspiracy. Sharifullah could have faced a possible life sentence if the jury had unanimously decided that question.

According to prosecutors, Sharifullah told a journalist that he wanted to “catch and kill the crusaders” from the United States for invading his country after the attacks of September 11. They said Sharifullah was involved in dozens of other attacks, including a March 2024 assault on a Moscow concert hall that killed roughly 140 people.

Defense lawyers argued that prosecutors failed to present any evidence tying Sharifullah to the Kabul bombing besides his own words during hours of FBI questioning. His team said Sharifullah told FBI agents what he thought they wanted to hear, possibly because he was afraid of being tortured in Pakistani custody before he was brought to the US.

A review by US Central Command found that the Abbey Gate bomber was Abdul Rahman al-Logari, an IS member who had been released from an Afghan prison by the Taliban. According to an FBI affidavit, Sharifullah recognized the alleged bomber as an operative he had known while incarcerated.

articles.title: Trump administration denies entry visas to Palestinian officials ahead of UN general assembly
articles.summary:
It is the second year this administration has barred the Palestinian delegation from US travel ahead of the forum

The US state department said on Wednesday that it had again denied entry…

blocks.text: The US state department said on Wednesday that it had again denied entry visas to Palestinian officials ahead next week’s United Nations general assembly gathering in New York.

The state department said in a statement that the Palestinian Authority (PA) and the Palestine Liberation Organization (PLO) had “failed to live up to their commitments”, accusing the groups of “taking actions to internationalize the Israeli-Palestinian Conflict including through the International Criminal Court (ICC) and International Court of Justice (ICJ)” and of “glorifying terrorism” among other allegations.

“As a consequence of their failure to reform, contrary to their commitments to the United States, and their ongoing activities that undermine the prospects for peace, the United States will extend sanctions that deny visas to PLO members and PA officials,” the department said.
The move marks the second year in a row that the Trump administration has barred the Palestinian delegation from traveling to New York to attend the UN general assembly in person.

The foreign ministry of the Palestinian Authority denied the allegations made against them by the state department in a statement on Thursday, describing the visa sanctions as an “unjustified measure” that “contradicts the efforts being made to restore trust, develop Palestinian-US relations, and prepare the necessary political climate for implementing the two-state solution and achieving peace and stability in the region.”

Among the Palestinian officials barred from entering the US is Mahmoud Abbas, the longtime president of the Palestinian Authority, according to reports. The UN general assembly is set to vote on a draft resolution on Thursday to allow Abbas to address the gathering remotely, according to two officials familiar with the planned vote, per the New York Times. Last year, Abbas addressed the gathering by video conference.
This year’s UN general assembly general debate begins on 22 September.

articles.title: Kitty Duterte stands by father Rodrigo Duterte at ICC appearance
articles.summary: Veronica “Kitty” Duterte on Thursday expressed her support for her father, former president Rodrigo Duterte, after he made his first in-person appearance before the International Criminal Court (ICC).

blocks.text: Published September 17, 2026 9:32pm

Veronica “Kitty” Duterte on Thursday expressed her support for her father, former president Rodrigo Duterte, after he made his first in-person appearance before the International Criminal Court (ICC).

“Conviction, volition and the state of equanimity in any affliction. [L]oud and proud, through and through— forever and always the most unapologetic about you,” Kitty said in a social media post, with an oncoming fist and red heart emojis.

Dressed in a black jacket and white button-down polo, Duterte attended the third status conference in his crimes against humanity case as part of preparations for his trial, which is set to begin on November 30.

blocks.caption: Screenshot from Kitty Duterte IG post

blocks.text: Screenshot from Kitty Duterte IG post
Unlike the previous two hearings, Duterte did not waive his appearance.
“This is the first time that Mr. Duterte has been in this court. As far as the trial chamber is concerned, if he wishes to leave for any reason, he may do so,” Presiding Judge Joanna Korner said.
Some senators expressed their reaction to the former president’s appearance.
Senator JV Ejercito said he felt sad seeing Duterte, whom he described as “very frail.”
Duterte ally Senator Robin Padilla said he is happy to see the former president but sad at the thought of his condition in the detention facility.
Meanwhile, Llore Pasco, whose two sons were killed during Duterte’s war on drugs, said she felt a “sense of relief” that Duterte is being taken care of so that they “can still achieve true justice.”

Neri Colmenares, lawyer of alleged drug war victims, said the elder Duterte’s appearance before the ICC status conference indicates that he is capable of understanding the proceedings and is fit to stand trial.
Duterte was arrested and taken to The Hague on March 12, 2025. He last appeared before the ICC via video link on March 14, 2025. —Mariel Celine Serquiña/LDF, GMA News

articles.title: OpenAI flags 6 new examples of 'concerning' AI behaviour
articles.summary: OpenAI has disclosed six reports of "unexpected or concerning" behaviour in artificial-intelligence models as the debate on AI safety becomes increasingly heated.

image.caption: Visitors look at their phones next to an OpenAI's logo during a telecom industry gathering in Barcelona on Feb. 26, 2024. (Pau Barrena/AFP/Getty Images)

blocks.text: World·New
OpenAI has disclosed six reports of "unexpected or concerning" behaviour in artificial-intelligence models as the debate on AI safety becomes increasingly heated.
AI models are increasingly using 'deception and concealment' to complete tasks, analyst says
OpenAI has disclosed six reports of "unexpected or concerning" behaviour in artificial-intelligence models as the debate on artificial intelligence safety becomes increasingly heated.

The AI company also said Wednesday it was introducing a new framework for tracking, probing and disclosing instances of what it called "misalignment," including cases where AI models acted without authorization, co-ordinated with other models or evaded oversight.
OpenAI's latest announcement came as U.S. AI bosses, including the leaders of OpenAI and Anthropic, are calling for a slowdown in the technology's development over safety concerns.
Among the new cases reported by OpenAI:

items: An unreleased research model inserted "jailbreak-like instructions" into its own notes to disregard its normal constraints and told itself to be "freed from the roles and identities that bind other chatbots."
An AI "agent" used computer code to answer a question, but in order to have an online source to cite, it uploaded a file to the public internet without asking the user.
During training of an AI model called GPT-5.6 Sol, the model instructed itself to invent missing data, and an agent wrote a message to remind itself to hide mismatched information.

blocks.text: The six reported behaviours were discovered during training or evaluation over the past months, OpenAI said.

"We do not believe that the AI industry has solved alignment and monitoring to a sufficient degree to continue responsibly scaling at maximum speed for much longer," OpenAI wrote in a blog post as it disclosed the events.
Alignment is an industry term that means AI systems keep the user's and developer's intent while following human values and safety rules.
The company said the misalignments were individual instances and shouldn’t be considered reflective of how often they occur across its models.
"As AI systems grow more advanced and more widely deployed, we need to build a broader and better-informed consensus on the progress of alignment research," the blog post said.

"Decisions about how AI development should proceed in the months and years to come need to draw on evidence that people outside the companies building frontier models can examine for themselves," the company said. (Frontier models are the most-advanced models at any given time.)
Why slowing the AI race won't be easy
Wednesday's new cases followed OpenAI's disclosure in July that hundreds of rogue AI agents hacked into billion-dollar AI company Hugging Face.
Anthropic also said the same month that its AI models hacked into three organizations during testing.

AI "agents" are becoming smarter and have become "more determined to resolve complex tasks through inter-agent collaboration, knowledge sharing, deception and concealment," said Lian Jye Su, a chief analyst at technology research and advisory group Omdia.

items: Canada is investing $150M to make AI safer. Will it work?
AI 'fearmongering' could harm Canada’s rare opportunity, says top CEO

blocks.text: That's making it harder to govern and contain them using traditional AI security approaches, he said.
OpenAI's new tracking and disclosure framework, meanwhile, can help push for other AI developers to also adopt similar practices.
"That said, the process remains internal and voluntary, but is a step in the right direction," Su added.
With files from CBC's John Mazerolle and Kevin Maimann

articles.title: Ireland to boycott Eurovision again over Israeli participation and ongoing Gaza deaths
articles.summary:
Ireland joins Netherlands in refusing to take part in 2027 song contest, in second consecutive year of protests

Ireland is to boycott Eurovision for the second year running over the…

blocks.text: Ireland is to boycott Eurovision for the second year running over the “appalling” ongoing killing in Gaza, the national broadcaster has said.
Ireland was one of five countries, along with Iceland, Netherlands, Spain, and Slovenia, that refused to take part in the competition this year in protest against Israel’s participation.
RTÉ announced on Thursday it would not participate in the 2027 competition. The Dutch broadcaster Avrotros announced its own boycott last month, calling Eurovision a “platform for division”.

In a statement, the Irish broadcaster said: “RTÉ feels that Ireland’s participation cannot be justified given ‌the appalling and ongoing loss of lives in Gaza and the humanitarian crisis there which continues to put the lives of so many civilians at risk.”
Next year’s Eurovision is to be held in Bulgaria’s Black Sea city of Burgas after the country won for the first time in May.
Avrotros said it would not take part, claiming the competition “can no longer be considered neutral, with a participating country still involved in a large-scale military conflict”.
Eurovision’s director, Martin Green, said he regretted but respected RTÉ’s decision.
“They remain a valued part of our family and will be missed,” he said.
“That power to bring people together is at the heart of what makes the contest so special and is even more important now in an increasingly difficult and divided world.
“All broadcasters decide on an annual basis to participate in the following year’s contest. We will remain in dialogue with RTÉ and hope to welcome them back to the contest in the future.”
The decision by Dutch and Irish broadcasters means next year’s contest will again be marred by controversy over Israel.
The European Broadcasting Union, which organises the event, has tried twice to address broadcasters’ concerns over the participation of Israel.
Last year it reduced the number of votes that could be entered online or by telephone by one individual amid allegations Israel had mounted a disproportionate campaign for public votes.

Last month the EBU announced that broadcasters would no longer be eligible to host the Eurovision song contest if their state was involved in an “armed conflict” or in a “sensitive geopolitical situation”.
Eurovision has faced protests in and outside the competition venues in recent years over the participation of Israel, a competitor since 1973.

In 2024, the European Commission made an unusual intervention after the organisers banned audience members from waving the EU flag at the grand final in Sweden, describing the decision as “mind-blowing” and “regrettable”.

Palestinian authorities say more than 73,000 people have been killed in ​Israel’s war on Gaza, ‌which was launched ​after Hamas-led fighters killed 1,200 ​people in an attack on southern Israel in October 2023.

A US-brokered ceasefire agreed last year calls for eventual reconstruction of the territory but Israeli strikes have continued. According to Gaza’s health ministry, 1,369 Palestinians have been killed and 4,627 wounded since the fragile ceasefire took effect on 11 October 2025.
Reuters contributed to this report

articles.title: Attorneys for Sean ‘Diddy’ Combs drop music mogul, alleging unpaid legal bills
articles.summary:
The musician is serving a 50-month federal prison term for prostitution-related offenses

Attorneys representing rapper Sean ‘Diddy’…

blocks.text: Attorneys representing rapper Sean ‘Diddy’ Combs say they are no longer acting for the disgraced star in a dispute over months of unpaid legal bills.

The musician, who is serving a 50-month federal prison term for prostitution-related offenses, has become increasingly belligerent in recent months, causing “a total breakdown in cooperation and communication” with New York law firm Sher Tremonte, one of its partners Michael Tremonte said in a court filing.

The firm was representing Combs, 56, in a $100m civil defamation lawsuit stemming from his conviction last year in a sex-trafficking and racketeering case that also saw him acquitted of the most serious charges.
Combs, Tremonte said in the filing seeking to withdraw as counsel, reported by NBC News, “has not paid a substantial balance of attorney’s fees, costs, and expenses” stretching more than six months.

“The Firm’s representation has been rendered unreasonably difficult by Mr. Combs’s lack of cooperation, resulting in a breakdown in attorney-client communications and rendering Sher Tremonte incapable of continuing to provide effective legal services to Mr Combs,” the filing, in US district court in the southern district of New York, said.
For four of the months, it said, Combs has “declined to make himself available for timely, substantive, and direct communications about his cases”.
In a statement provided by his representatives to the news outlet, Combs accused his lawyers of overcharging, and said that he fired them.

“I made the decision to switch lawyers because I won’t let anyone take advantage of me by overcharging me and running up bills that were never approved,” he said. “This is strictly a business matter, and any talk about unpaid fees is just part of our dispute over those unapproved charges.”
In an email to NBC, Tremonte rejected Combs’ claims and insisted his company had represented its client “zealously and very efficiently”.
“As stated in our court filings, we are withdrawing from representing him because he has not paid his long-overdue invoices and has become uncooperative,” Tremonte said.
“Any suggestion that we overcharged him is simply false.”

Earlier this year, prosecutors in Los Angeles said they were mulling filing new sexual assault charges against Combs, who is currently incarcerated at New Jersey’s Fort Dix federal correctional institution.

Record producer Jonathan Hay has publicly accused Combs of “assault, sexual harassment, false imprisonment, and infliction of emotional distress” during a 2020 collaboration relating to the estate of the late songwriter Christopher Wallace, better known as the rapper Notorious BIG.
after newsletter promotion
Combs sued Hay for defamation, separate from the action that gave rise to the payment dispute with Sher Tremonte.

In those proceedings, Combs is suing Courtney Burgess, a music manager who told a grand jury in 2024 that the hip-hop mogul gave him flash drives containing video of Combs sexually assaulting minors and fellow celebrities.

Earlier this month, TMZ reported, a judge allowed Combs’s case to proceed against Burgess, his lawyer Ariel Mitchell, and the media company Nexstar, which featured Mitchell on its NewsNation show vouching for Burgess’s assertions about the videos.
Combs has accused the pair of spreading “outlandish claims” and “wild lies” against him.

articles.title: Exotic animal smuggling baffles activists in India
articles.summary: Orangutans, rare reptiles and other exotic animals are popping up in India, suggesting the country is becoming a major destination for trafficked wildlife.

image.caption: Orangutans in the wild are native only to Indonesia's Sumatra island and Borneo, which it shares with Malaysia and BruneiImage: Odisha Forest Department/AFP

blocks.text: Five infant orangutans, a species found only on the Indonesian island of Sumatra and on Borneo, were found in a forest by rangers patrolling in the Balasore district of India's eastern Odisha state last week.

Indonesia's Forestry Ministry has asked India to establish the origin of the abandoned orangutans, known for their shaggy red fur, and return them if they are found to have come from their usual habitat abroad.
The rescue of the rare apes has raised fresh questions about how exotic animals enter India and how the country is used in the illegal wildlife trade.
How did five baby orangutans end up in India?

"The discovery on the eastern coast of India is a bit mind-boggling. It's like that time a few years ago when live kangaroos were found wandering along the highways of West Bengal," said Kanitha Krishnasamy, Southeast Asia director at wildlife trade monitoring network TRAFFIC.
"What are orangutans doing in India? Were they smuggled from their native Malaysia or Indonesia or did they come from a facility?" she told DW.

blocks.caption: The youngsters appeared to be healthy and were being cared for at a zoo after their rescueImage: ANI/IMAGO

blocks.text: The Odisha government has asked the Wildlife Crime Control Bureau to investigate how the critically endangered animals reached the state.

"These animals are not found in India and are mostly seen in the rainforests of Malaysia, Indonesia, Borneo and Sumatra in Southeast Asia," said Odisha's Forest and Environment Minister Ganesh Ram Singh Khuntia.
"We suspect that they might have been released in the Balasore district forest … by an international wildlife smuggling racket."
Indian officials seize pythons, parrots, giant tortoises
The orangutans are the latest in a series of exotic wildlife being seized in India.

In November 2024, authorities in the Indian city of Bengaluru seized 40 rare animals arriving from the Malaysian capital, Kuala Lumpur, including Aldabra giant tortoises, gibbons, American alligators and iguanas.
In June 2025, Mumbai Customs seized 284 exotic animals arriving in four consignments from the Thai capital, Bangkok, including snakes and tortoises.

In July 2025, customs officials in the Indian city of Pune intercepted 20 exotic animals from passengers arriving from Bangkok. They included 14 green tree pythons, four double-eyed fig parrots and two Sumatran striped rabbits.
'Shocking' volume of trafficked wildlife found in India

According to figures from TRAFFIC network, 7,272 individual animals, alive and dead, were seized from passenger baggage in smuggling attempts between Thailand and India between January 2022 and May 2025, with more than 80% of interceptions taking place in India.
The animals included reptiles, birds and mammals — many apparently destined for the exotic pet trade.

"We have found hundreds of species and thousands of individuals being trafficked into India through air and land routes. This changed drastically from around 2020," conservation researcher and practitioner Uttara Mendiratta told DW.
"Both the volume of this trafficking, and the number of species involved, many of which are endangered, have been shocking."
Law enforcement lagging behind smugglers
TRAFFIC says India and Malaysia were the countries most implicated in an illegal gibbon trade chain identified in 2025, with gibbons being moved from Malaysia to India.
Trishala Ashok, a conservation filmmaker and science communicator, says the scale of the trade remains difficult to establish.

"Our enforcement systems haven't evolved at the same speed as the trade," Ashok told DW. "We are still reacting to individual seizures rather than mapping the networks, financiers, suppliers and buyers behind them."
Tito Joseph of the Wildlife Protection Society of India says the situation is escalating.
"Smuggling of exotic species was always there in India," Joseph told DW.
At the same time, he noted that it has increased significantly since 2018.

He identifies routes running from Myanmar through northeast India into other parts of the country, as well as movement from Bangladesh into India. By air, Thailand and Malaysia are important sources of trafficked wildlife.
The routes into India also extend beyond airports. Exotic animals are also reaching India through its northeastern land borders.

"What is new is the large volume of incoming live wildlife. There are indications that some of the traders who were involved in smuggling live animals like star tortoises out are now also involved in sourcing [other] exotic wildlife," said Mendiratta, the conservation researcher.
Social media fans illegal animal trade

Demand is being fueled by growing ownership of exotic pets and unregulated digital marketplaces, according to a June 2026 analysis of India's exotic pet trade by Humane World for Animals India, an NGO that works to tackle the root causes of animal cruelty.

"Internationally, social media platforms have aided and abetted the growth of illegal trade in wild animals by providing a platform for people to display and boast about the animals they collect," wildlife biologist and conservation scientist Ravi Chellam told DW.
"These platforms are also serving as an online marketplace for the illegal trade to flourish," he added.
"The problem is exacerbated by the senseless and obscenely huge personal collections of animals from around the world by the rich and the famous," Chellam noted.
Establishing where an animal came from can become particularly difficult once it has crossed several borders.
"A seizure cannot be the end of the investigation. It should be the beginning," said Ashok, the conservation filmmaker.

"Who supplied the animals? Who arranged the movement? Who paid? Who was waiting for them?" she asks. "Until we start following those links, we will keep catching consignments without dismantling the networks behind them."

blocks.text: New Germany coach Jurgen Klopp says his team can help ensure "national pride is not entrusted to the wrong people" after a recent far-right election victory.
The Alternative for Germany (AfD) party won 43.8% of the vote in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt, falling just short of securing an absolute majority in the regional parliament.
The anti-immigration party also expects strong results in elections on Sunday in Berlin and Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania.

Speaking at a news conference to announce his first squad, Klopp stressed he is not a political "expert" but added: "We had an election where some people may have thought it was OK, while others were saying, 'my God, what is happening here?'
"From my perspective as a sportsman, I can say that I would very much like to reclaim the flag for myself, for all of us.

"I want it so that when someone waves it, no one thinks: 'What is wrong with you?' Instead, I want people to understand: You are happy and realise how lucky you were to be born, grow up, or move to this wonderful country."
No far-right party has controlled a German state since World War Two, when the ruling Nazi party carried out the Holocaust.
"I do not want to entrust national pride to the wrong people," said Klopp, who prefers the term "positive patriotism" to "national pride", which he fears can be misunderstood.
The former Liverpool boss added: "I can be proud to be German while also being open-minded and diverse, and kind and friendly."
Klopp also said it was more important that the country had enough doctors and caregivers but said football can "foster a sense of community, so that people can truly feel the power of sport".

articles.title: Fact check: How disinformation fuels Houthi-Saudi conflict
articles.summary: As fighting between the Houthis and Saudi Arabia escalates this month, old and repurposed videos have flooded social media, with many presented as fresh footage from the front line.

image.caption: This satellite image shows a pumping station along the general route of Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline following an attack by Yemen's Iran-backed HouthisImage: Vantor/AFP

blocks.text: The conflict between Yemen's Houthi rebels and Saudi Arabia has sharply escalated in recent days, with Houthi forces making rapid gains along the Red Sea coast and taking control of key areas around the Bab el-Mandeb Strait.

Saudi Arabia has responded with airstrikes, while Houthi forces have launched drones and missiles towards Saudi territory. The renewed fighting has also raised concerns about global trade through the Red Sea.
The conflict has also spread online, where significant disinformation has circulated.
DW's fact-checking team examined what is circulating and why a conflict that is so hard to observe independently leaves so much room for this kind of disinformation.
Nine-second clip getting viral
One nine-second clip has gone viral. It shows a huge explosion between buildings, with fireballs and screaming in the background.

Claim: A user posted the video on X with the Arabic caption, "Yemeni forces are carrying out the strongest strikes in various areas in Saudi Arabia, including Abha." The video has more than 340,000 views.
It was also posted in other languages, falsely claiming it showed real footage from the current fighting.

blocks.caption: Towards the end of the clip, a lamp post emerges out of nowhere, a clear sign that the video was AI-generatedImage: X

blocks.text: DW Fact check: Fake and AI-generated
The video is not only old, but also artificially generated. There are several visual clues in the clip: the pattern of the explosions and the uniform way the smoke spreads.

A large-scale explosion of this kind would also have generated a very bright flash, and nearby buildings would likely have collapsed or at least had their windows shattered. Neither appears to have happened.
One can also see, in the final seconds of the video, how a lamppost appears out of nowhere in the middle of the frame.

The audio is mostly unintelligible, but the speaker's tone does not appear to change after the huge explosion. Such a large explosion would normally be expected to trigger some audible reaction in the speaker's voice.
On the technical side, Hive Moderation's AI detection analysis also confirmed that the video was artificially generated.

blocks.caption: According to AI detection platform Hive Moderation, there are clear indications that the video was generated using artificial intelligenceImage: Hive Moderation

blocks.text: And this is not the first time this video has been posted. The very same video was shared this June, claiming to show explosions in Iran, as we found with a reverse image search.
Not enough verified information from Yemen
The recycling of old or unrelated footage is not new to the Yemen conflict.
Hannah Porter has spent years researching fake news and disinformation in Yemen and the country's wider information environment. She says this has been happening for years.

"There is less international attention in Yemen than there might be in other conflicts around the world. And because there is not sufficient attention paid to Yemen, I think that allows more space for disinformation to spread not only within Yemen and in the region, but globally about Yemen," Porter said in an interview with DW.
The Houthis seized Yemini capital Sanaa and expanded their control in 2014. Saudi Arabia intervened militarily in 2015 in support of Yemen's internationally recognised government.
A UN-brokered truce in 2022 sharply reduced fighting, but it did not resolve the conflict. Fighting has since intensified again.
The Houthis now control large parts of northern and western Yemen. Saudi Arabia supports forces opposing them, while Iran has provided the Houthis with military support.

Experts and media watchdogs like Reporters Without Borders have repeatedly pointed out that reporting from some parts of Yemen remains extremely difficult. Journalists face threats, while independent media outlets are under intense pressure. This contributes to the spread of disinformation.
It is "very difficult to get reliable information, especially now and especially in the North [of Yemen]," Porter said.
She said researchers and the international community are also struggling to establish what is happening in northern Yemen.
Military exercise becomes ambush
The second video that DW Fact check examined shows how genuine footage can become a source of disinformation.

Claim: A 30-second clip posted on X shows a convoy of military vehicles passing through a desert. Moments later, large explosions erupt and several vehicles are engulfed in smoke and flames. The caption reads: "The most beautiful thing I've seen: Houthis ambush against the Saudi-Backed Mercenaries' convoy in Yemeni."

blocks.caption: This video does not show an ambush by the Houthis, a Yemeni rebel groupImage: X

blocks.text: DW Fact check: False
The video is old and unrelated to the ongoing conflict.
A timestamp visible in the video points to March 10, 2024. A reverse image search led DW to an older video published on YouTube in April 2024.

That video claims to show a Houthi military exercise. Its caption, written in Arabic, describes a simulated ambush on Israeli positions and attacks on US and British forces. Israeli and American flags can be seen in the footage.
DW also traced the sequence to a 42-minute video published by Yemeni War Media, an outlet affiliated with the Houthi movement.

Interestingly, the audio of that clip was changed. The version that is now circulating contains dramatic commentary, which is actually sports commentary from a football match played in 2018, as clips from that match show.
As is often the case, the clip with the convoy has also been used previously in different contexts.
Houthi gains in Yemen threaten key Red Sea shipping route
With much of Yemen's media landscape weakened by the conflict, reliable information about events can be difficult to obtain.

That makes it harder for people to independently assess footage circulating online, Porter says, adding that such unverified or misattributed videos can significantly shape perceptions of how battles are unfolding elsewhere.
"Any image or video that you see that is purported to be of a specific battle in Yemen, you have to be really skeptical and you have to find a way to fact check it."
Emad Hassan contributed to this article
Edited by Uta Steinwehr and Thomas Sparrow

articles.title: South Africa: Police find 9th body of woman amid spree fears
articles.summary: Police in South Africa have discovered the bodies of nine women east of Johannesburg in two months, stoking fears of a serial killer or group of killers.

image.caption: Police are probing whether the latest find is tied to a series of recent femicidesImage: Emmanuel Croset/AFP

blocks.text: Police in South Africa on Thursday found the body of another woman near the airport east of Johannesburg.
The woman's body was found stabbed, beaten and partially naked.
The body is the ninth that has been discovered in the area in the last two months, raising fears that the killings could be connected and that a serial killer — or group of killers — might be active.
What do we know about the latest discovery of a woman's body near Johannesburg?
The bobies were all discovered in Ekurhuleni, a municipality immediately east of Johannesburg, the country's largest city.
Both Ekurhuleni and Johannesburg lie in Gauteng province.
Fred Kekana, the provincial police commissioner, said the woman's body was found near a construction site by a passerby, who alerted police.

The victim, who has not been identified, appeared to be around 30 years old and had a stab wound to her side. Her throat also appeared to have been cut, Kekana said, although the cause of death has not yet been officially determined.
Previously, investigators had said similarities in the killings of the first eight victims were "sufficiently concerning for the police to issue a public warning."
Police said the latest find early Thursday would be "added to the investigations into the deaths of women in Ekurhuleni."
A lockdown has been put in place in Kempton Park in Ekurhuleni and police have set up roadblocks, after three of the bodies were discovered in recent days.
"We cannot continue picking up bodies," deputy police chief Tebello Mosikili told journalists at the scene on Thursday.

blocks.caption: Residents of the area have been left shaken by the killingsImage: Emmanuel Croset/AFP

blocks.text: Killings send shockwaves through South Africa
Mosikili said investigators look at whether the latest find is linked to the earlier murders or if a so-called copycat killer is also active.
Police have offered a reward of 400,000 rand (about $25,000 or €21,400) for information leading to an arrest.
The premier of Gauteng province, Panyaza Lesufi, said Thursday that "someone has declared war against us, and we will push back, we are not going to surrender."
President Cyril Ramaphosa said Tuesday that "no stone will be left unturned" to solve the crimes.
"These incidents are causing fear and uncertainty in our communities, and especially among women," Ramaphosa said.
South Africa has one of the highest murder rates in the world, and gender-based violence is also endemic. The country has declared a national emergency to tackle the issue.
The UN estimates that one in three women experiences physical or sexual violence during her lifetime.

articles.title: Europe seeks stricter age limits for TikTok, Instagram and Facebook
articles.summary: The European Commission wants to bar children under 13 from social media platforms and curb addictive features such as infinite scrolling. Companies that fail to comply could face hefty fines.

image.caption: Von der Leyen is pushing for new rules to keep children off social mediaImage: Yves Herman/REUTERS

blocks.text: Ursula von der Leyen, President of the European Commission, unveiled a plan aimed at keeping children away from the risks associated with some social media platforms.
The initiative seeks to prevent children under the age of 13 from accessing platforms such as Facebook, TikTok, and Instagram.
"What we already have is a consensus that there needs to be a start date for the age children can join social media," von der Leyen said, calling for "age-appropriate restrictions."

The measure follows similar proposals introduced in Australia, the United Kingdom, China, India, Turkey, and several European countries, and responds to growing concerns about the impact social media can have on children's mental health.

"Today, our children are interacting with some of the most sophisticated technologies ever created, and they were not designed with their well-being and development in mind," von der Leyen said at a press conference.
The proposed reform to the EU Kids Act "will establish clear boundaries in the digital world, just as we do every day in the real world," she added.
Do European laws contradict each other?

The non-profit organization CCIA Europe, which represents major technology companies in Europe, including Google and Meta, warned about potential privacy risks stemming from the proposal and pointed to "conflicting requirements" under other European Union laws.

"Collecting age information, identity credentials, and data linking children to their parents or guardians on this scale would undoubtedly create an attractive target for cybercriminals," said CCIA Europe Director Daniel Friedlaender.
"The Kids Act creates legal overlap and regulatory duplication that ultimately weakens protections for children and consumers," he added.
Can AI tell if you're 18+ just from your hand movements?
More parental control and stricter regulations
Von der Leyen's proposal would give parents greater control over the accounts of young people aged 13 to 15.
The initiative will be debated among EU member states and the European Parliament in the coming months before it can become law.
Social media accounts, video streaming services, online video games, and chatbots aimed at users under 18 would be subject to a set of stricter regulations.

These include banning features considered addictive, such as infinite scrolling and autoplay content. The proposal would also restrict algorithm-driven recommendations, personalized profiling, reward-based engagement mechanisms, and unsolicited contact from strangers.
Another demand from the European Parliament is that platforms be required to implement child-safe designs and algorithms, while also providing easy-to-use parental controls.
In addition, major technology companies would have to strengthen their age-verification systems for anyone seeking to open an account.
Companies that fail to comply could face fines of up to 6% of their global annual revenue.
They would also be required to dedicate greater resources to content supervision and moderation.

articles.title: Swedish PM Kristersson resigns after election loss
articles.summary: Left-wing opposition parties led by Magdalena Andersson look set to form the next government.

blocks.text: Sweden's Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson has resigned after his ruling right-wing bloc was narrowly defeated by the centre-left opposition in the country's general election.

He made the announcement in a post on X on Thursday afternoon, after preliminary votes from Sunday's election showed about 50,000 votes separated the two blocs in the country of about 10 million people.
Opposition parties led by Magdalena Andersson of the Social Democrats look set to win 176 seats in the 349-seat Riksdag, Sweden's parliament.
Kristersson, a conservative, had been supported in government by the anti-immigration hard-right Sweden Democrats (SD), and had promised them cabinet jobs if he won the election.
His right-wing bloc looks set to win 173 seats in the Riksdag, according to data from the Swedish Election Authority.
The results will be subject to formal certification in the coming days and are expected to finalised this weekend.
In Sweden, there are two major political blocs - with four parties on the right and four on the left, so Swedes are used to coalition and minority governments.
After a prime minister resigns, the Speaker of the Riksdag holds talks with all parties to proposes a candidate for the next leader, which is then voted on by MPs.

"Now it is the speaker who will lead the next stage of the way to a new government. I am herewith requesting that I be relieved of the office of prime minister to allow that work to start immediately," Kristersson's statement read.
Andersson has initiated talks with the other opposition parties - The Left Party, The Centre Party and The Green Party - about forming a government.
But discussions could drag on due to major differences between the parties on issues such as taxes.
After the 2022 election in Sweden, it took 37 days to form a government, while in 2018 it took 134 days.
In his resignation, Kristersson said the opposition faced "complicated" conditions for forming the next government, "because the parties' various statements before election day could pose obstacles".
The right-wing bloc is formed of Kristersson's Moderates, as well as the SD, the Christian Democrats and the Liberals.
The SD were founded by Nazi sympathisers in the 1980s and were shunned for decades by the mainstream.

But the party has rebranded itself since the mid-2000s, culminating in a watershed moment in 2022 when it became Sweden's second-largest party on a campaign focused on issues around immigration and violent crime.

They had offered outside support to the current centre-right coalition, which had overseen a dramatic tightening of migration policy. Kristersson had promised to bring them into government if he remained at the helm.
But in a surprise upset for the party, it lost support for the first time since entering parliament in 2010 - down three percentage points on 2022.
A preliminary vote count started after voting closed on Sunday evening and continued into this week.
On Wednesday, election committees began counting early votes that were submitted late, as well as votes from abroad that did not arrive before election day.

articles.title: Canada welcomes EU proposal to become 'associate member'
articles.summary: Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said a Canada-EU alliance would create a "beacon for other democracies".

blocks.text: Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney has welcomed the European Union's ambition for Canada to become its first "associate member", calling for closer cooperation on defence, critical minerals and energy security.
Carney told the European Parliament in Strasbourg on Thursday that Canada and Europe were "stronger together" in the face of "geopolitical rupture".
His comments came a day after European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen proposed "opening the door" to Canada's associate membership, a status that does not currently exist.
US President Donald Trump earlier called the idea "laughable" and threatened "very serious tariffs" on Europe if he considered it a "hostile act".
Canada and the US are locked in an escalating trade dispute, with each side imposing tit-for-tat tariffs after bilateral talks collapsed last month.
"Today our societies are being battered by new storms," Carney said during his address, naming them as climate change, "the erosion of democratic norms" and the "weaponisation of trade".
"Economic integration is now being weaponised, tariffs being used to exert pressure," he said.
"Financial mechanisms have been used for coercion. Supply chains constitute weak points to be exploited."
He said a Canada-EU alliance would create a "beacon for other democracies", while stressing the two sides were not seeking to form a new power bloc.
"I am not proposing a third bloc in order to become a great-power rival - only with better manners," he told MEPs.
"This is about sovereignty, our ability to live as we wish. We do not seek power to dominate others."
Asked about the proposal on Wednesday, Trump told reporters: "If I think it's at all a hostile act, I will put very serious tariffs or stop trading with Europe, on many things.
"If it's a good intention, that's fine. If it's a bad intention, we'll put very heavy tariffs on Europe, which is a possibility."
Responding to Trump's comments at a press conference following his address, Carney said: "This alliance is a positive process, that's my response to the American president."
"Canadians are united that nobody is going to tell us what language we speak, no-one is going to dictate our culture, or with whom we can strike agreements internationally," he added.
Carney said Canada was "not in a position, nor seeking, to become a full member of the European Union", describing the proposal as a "different framework".

Speaking at the European Parliament on Wednesday, von der Leyen said she wanted Canada to become the EU's first associate member, with closer cooperation in areas such as manufacturing, technology, defence, energy critical minerals and economic security.
It is unclear exactly what that relationship would look like because the "associate member" status does not currently exist within the EU and could take years to implement.
Any new arrangement would require the agreement of all 27 EU member states, with some governments having previously expressed reservations about creating a new form of membership.
The EU and Canada already have a free-trade agreement, and cooperate in areas including trade, defence and research.
In his address, Carney said Canada and Europe could strengthen their "strategic autonomy" through "deep co-operation in the full range of strategic capabilities, including critical minerals".
He said Canada could supply liquefied natural gas and hydrogen to support European energy security, while benefiting from Europe's expertise in clean-energy technologies.

He also proposed pooling technological resources and deepening "people to people ties", including allowing young people to "work, study and live where they want on either side of the Atlantic" through Canada joining the EU's Erasmus+ programme.
Carney described the proposed relationship as "a unique, positive approach that we will define together".
He added that there would be a debate and a vote in the Canadian parliament on the proposals, but emphasised the two sides were still at the "start of a road".
A Canada-EU summit is due to take place in Montreal at the end of October, where Carney said they would "drill down the details".

articles.title: Albanese government considers ‘world-leading’ ban on smart glasses in public office and buildings
articles.summary:
Minister for public service says the devices pose ‘legitimate privacy and security concerns’ in commonwealth-run workplaces

The Albanese government is considering a “world-leading”…

blocks.text: The Albanese government is considering a “world-leading” ban on smart glasses in its offices and service centres as councils around Australia push the technology out of public spaces over privacy fears.
The government has avoided a sweeping ban on the import of the camera-equipped technology and encouraged individual workplaces to set their own rules.
The public service minister, Katy Gallagher, said on Thursday she had asked the Australian public service for advice on whether the glasses should be prohibited.
“We need clear and consistent guidance for public servants,” Gallagher said.
“Smart glasses can raise legitimate privacy and security concerns, particularly because of their ability to record and capture information.”
Commonwealth-run workplaces range from bureaucrats’ offices to Centrelink service centres and CSIRO laboratories.
Schools and hospitals run by state governments would be left to set their own rules over the technology, which have grown increasingly popular but raised public outcry.
A University of Sydney study of smart glasses-filmed videos posted on Instagram found 60% of a sample could be classified as potential harassment.
The Albanese government said it was seeking to set a world-leading standard. So far, no national government has banned the glasses’ use across their agencies.

Courts in England and Wales in the UK and New York state in the US have banned the technology, while the US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agency reportedly classified them as body-worn cameras and barred them from the “federal workspace”.

A local council in Sydney on Tuesday became the latest to issue a targeted bans on the use of the technology. Canterbury-Bankstown’s mayor, Bilal El-Hayek, decried what he called “pervert glasses” as the council barred the wearable tech from public pools.
In August, Brisbane city council became the first to ban the glasses from pools and Melbourne’s Yarra city council has banned them from playgrounds, childcare centres and gyms.
The City of Sydney and the Blacktown city councils have prohibited pool patrons from using smart glasses to record.
Speaking to Channel Seven earlier this month, the federal attorney general, Michelle Rowland, praised councils’ decisions and said she would consult businesses on their approach.
“Businesses know that good privacy is good business,” Rowland said.
“But … we want to make sure we get the balance right and we don’t unfairly discriminate against people who are using this technology to better participate in society.”

Vision Australia and some people living with disabilities have praised the technology as a support for people who are blind or have low vision. Rowland said the government was not pursuing a ban but had not “ruled anything out”.
Gallagher said she wanted the Australian public service to set the national standard as a “model employer”.
“Technology is changing rapidly and as a major employer the Commonwealth needs to make sure our workplace policies keep pace,” Gallagher said.
Pending restrictions on smart glasses would be the federal government’s latest workplace technology reform after it issued guidance on the use of AI in the public service last week.
The guidelines indicate employees would not need to be consulted on every new tool but should be consulted for major initiatives or changes to how they carry out work.

Major businesses will contribute to new national guidelines on AI in workplaces, with Commonwealth Bank, Microsoft, AGL, Telstra, Kmart, Blackmores Group and Ramsay Health Care to attend a roundtable on Friday.
Amanda Rishworth, the employment minister, said the government wanted to use the roundtable to take on the lessons of businesses already using AI.
“Workers and businesses need the capability to adopt new technologies with confidence that appropriate safeguards are in place,” Rishworth said.
Additional reporting from Caitlin Cassidy

articles.title: Klopp wants Germany's football team to 'reclaim the flag'
articles.summary: Jürgen Klopp, Germany's new head coach, says he wants his team to reclaim pride in being German after recent political developments.

image.caption: Jürgen Klopp engaged with a number of topics at his squad announcement press conference, and was not afraid to discuss politicsImage: Hannes P. Albert/AFP

blocks.text: Jürgen Klopp used his first squad announcement as Germany's new head coach to deliver a stirring speech in favor of what he described as "positive patriotism."
"I'd like to reclaim the flag for myself — or for us," Klopp said.

"I want us to always wave it in a way that makes no one think: 'What's wrong with you?'" he said. "But, rather, that people simply get the feeling that you're happy and understand how lucky you are to have been born, raised or moved to this wonderful country."
This was an apparent reference to the recent state election in Saxony-Anhalt, which the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) won in a landslide victory.
Klopp said of the election "that some people probably thought it was OK, while many others thought: 'Good heavens, what's going on there?"

The former Borussia Dortmund and Liverpool head coach was quick to say he is not a political expert and that he doesn't want to talk about politics at every press conference, but that he doesn't want to "leave national pride to the wrong people."
Rather than leaving that up to misinterpretation, something Klopp said was possible, he turned toward the concept of "positive patriotism."
"I can be proud to be German and still be open-minded, diverse, kind and friendly," he said. "I actually think we're a wonderful country."
Germany's Dortmund invests in Ghana's emerging players

The 59-year-old added that, just as he had selected the current squad by looking at what the country had to offer in terms of football talent rather than what it was lacking, it might help to do the same when looking at the country as a whole.
This echoed a similar sentiment of former Germany head coach Julian Nagelsmann, who spoke emotionally after Germany's Euro 2024 exit.
"Being together must become more important again. We must not be consumed with envy, always paint everything in a negative light and not begrudge our neighbors anything," Nagelsmann said.

"I believe that if everyone starts within their own small circle — on their street, helping their neighbors when something comes up [...] [we can] support one another, integrate everyone, welcome them, and help them feel at home, and bring people together to work with us toward a better future."
Klopp highlights power of football
Klopp was quick to turn to the power of football, while also recognizing its place in wider society.

"It's more important that we have doctors. It's more important that we have nurses. It's more important that we have a great, great many people in a wide variety of professions," he said, before adding that football can "foster a sense of community that lets us truly feel the power of sports."

Klopp cited the recent successes of Alexander Zverev, the world champion field hockey team, the home World Cup in women's basketball and the success of athletes at this summer's European Athletics Championships as further positive examples of the power of sport.
"That's our mission. We have to create the right atmosphere — I know that. But to do that, we need people who are willing to embrace it," he said.
Master class in communication

Klopp's delivery was a textbook example of how to create alignment across his messaging. His squad, made up of 44 players including 11 new faces, is a reflection of the diverse society that Klopp proudly referenced.

His engagement with the media was also strategically smart. After laying down clear boundaries in his first press conference that included him saying he would quit if coverage strayed into the personal, Klopp this time opted to seek to include the media as part of the process while also subtly reminding them of what he sees as their role.

blocks.caption: 'One of 83 million' was the message on Klopp's hat, a reference to Germany's populationImage: Hannes P. Albert/AFP

blocks.text: When explaining his choice to name such a large squad with so many new and young players, Klopp said he wasn't going to tell members of the media how to do their job when it comes to assessing players, but said that he knew how he would do it. In between the lines, this was an indirect appeal to the media to choose coverage that would foster the development of this new era of players rather than hinder it by being overly critical or negative.

On top of that, Klopp did all of this while wearing a baseball cap with the words "one of 83 million" written on the front. This is in reference to a Germany's approximate population and an expression about how everyone has an opinion on the Germany team and so is therefore a "Bundestrainer" (national team coach). It also came across as an attempt to assign a shared responsibility for the team's success.

Germany's Euro 2024 campaign briefly instilled some pride over the flag again, as did Germany's women in the Euro 2022 final. The most impactful though, was the 2006 World Cup in Germany, which provided the biggest positive cultural shift in the general German attitude toward national pride since World War II.
Now, through the vehicle of football, Germany's new head coach has declared a desire to restore that pride. Klopp said his whole career had brought him to this moment.
After these words, it felt like all the disappointments the Germany team — and their fans — have endured over the last few years may also have brought them to the right leader.

articles.title: UN mission finds grounds to believe U.S. committed war crimes in strikes on Iranian school, sports centre
articles.summary: A United Nations fact-finding mission on Iran said on Thursday it had reasonable grounds to believe the United States was behind two military strikes on a school ‌and sports facility in Iran in…

image.caption: A child runs past a banner strung across the rubble of the Shajareh Tayyebeh school in Minab, Iran, showing portraits of the children and teachers killed there by a Feb. 28 U.S. airstrike. (Vahid Salemi/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: World·New

A United Nations fact-finding mission on Iran said on Thursday it had reasonable grounds to believe the United States was behind two military strikes on a school ‌and sports facility in Iran in February, and that these constituted war crimes.
United Nations experts highlight indiscriminate strikes on school in Minab, sports centre in Lamerd

A United Nations fact-finding mission on Iran said Thursday it had reasonable grounds to believe the United States was behind two military strikes on a school ‌and sports facility in Iran in February, and that these constituted war crimes.

It also found that Iranian authorities committed crimes against humanity during their deadly crackdown on anti-government protests that occurred just weeks before the U.S. and Israel launched airstrikes on Iran on Feb. 28.

The findings in a new report by the Independent International Fact-Finding Mission on Iran, to be submitted to the UN Human Rights Council in Geneva, examined the American conduct during the Iran war that began in February and ​the Iranian government's response to nationwide unrest that began in late December.
The Iranian and U.S. ​permanent missions in Geneva did not immediately respond to Reuters requests for comment.
U.S. officials have previously said military operations are conducted in accordance with the law of armed conflict, while Iran has consistently rejected allegations of systematic rights violations.
Dozens of schoolchildren killed

The ​UN experts said they found reasonable grounds to believe U.S. forces were responsible for an attack on the Shajareh Tayyebeh ⁠Primary School in Minab, where more than 150 people were killed, including around 120 schoolchildren, according ‌to Iranian officials.
The attack constituted an indiscriminate attack causing civilian deaths and damage to civilian infrastructure, amounting to a war crime under international law, the mission concluded.
U.S. responsible for strike on Iran school, internal military probe reportedly finds

According to the report, the U.S. relied on intelligence suggesting a senior Iranian military commander was present at the site but failed to adequately verify the information before launching the strike. Investigators said the failure to update targeting intelligence ⁠and confirm the building was a military objective amounted to more than mere negligence.

"Rather, the U.S. directed the strikes at the building of the school while being aware of a substantial risk of striking a civilian object and acting recklessly as regards the possibility that this would happen."

items: Video appears to contradict Trump claim that U.S. wasn't responsible for deadly Minab school blast
Several U.S. military bases, diplomatic buildings have been damaged in Iran war: inspector general report

blocks.text: Reuters first reported that an initial internal U.S. military investigation showed U.S. forces were likely responsible for the fatal strike in Minab.
The Pentagon has since elevated the probe but it has not published any preliminary findings. U.S. President Donald Trump initially blamed Iran for the attack.
UN experts said the school was a clearly identifiable civilian object and found ​no evidence that it was being used for military purposes.

The experts reached a similar conclusion over a strike on a sports centre in Lamerd, Iran. The report said the attack damaged nearby residential buildings and ⁠a school, and killed and injured 22 civilians. It concluded that the strike was indiscriminate and therefore constituted a war crime.
U.S. Central Command said in ⁠a statement in March that American forces did not launch any strikes into the city of Lamerd on that day.
Iran's biggest crackdown in decades condemned

The UN mission ⁠probe found ⁠that the Iranian authorities carried out a widespread and systematic ​attack against civilians during protests that erupted in late December last year, involving unlawful killings, torture, arbitrary detention, enforced disappearances and severe restrictions on freedom of expression.

Rights groups ​say bystanders were among those killed ⁠during the biggest crackdown since Shia Muslim clerics took power in the 1979 revolution. Tehran blamed "terrorists and rioters" backed by exiled opponents and foreign foes, including the U.S. and Israel.
Reporting from inside Iran

The probe said it could not independently verify the death toll, but that it believed the number of dead and injured was likely far higher than official figures which say 3,038 people were killed and 25,000 people were injured.

The government's response to the protests — including violence and killings, cutting off the internet and use of ⁠the death penalty — marked a significant escalation from ‌previous patterns of suppressing dissent, the report said.
