articles.title: Jews once lived lived here: When houses tell stories
articles.summary: Time and again, residents tracing the history of their homes discover the lives of Jewish predecessors who fled or were deported amid stories of suffering and loss.

image.caption: A 1930 photograph of Salomo Birnbaum (standing) and his family, who had to leave their home in Germany and flee to London Image: David Birnbaum/Nathan & Solomon Birnbaum Archives, Toronto

blocks.text: Over the years, many people have passed through this fourth-floor apartment in an old Berlin building. Here, at Rosenheimer Straße 40, they have sat on the sofa and gathered around the kitchen table. They have looked out the window and let their minds wander.

Marie Rolshoven has lived here with her family since 2007. "The feeling of crossing that threshold, the same one the former residents crossed for the last time, stays with you," she says. She knows that Jews once lived here, and none of them survived the Nazi era.
Driven from their homes

After the National Socialists seized power in January 1933, it quickly became clear that Jews were considered second-class citizens under Nazi rule. Even the right to remain in their homes could no longer be taken for granted.

"A racially conscious fellow citizen cannot be expected to share a household with a Jew," the Nazi party newspaper Völkischer Beobachter wrote on September 18, 1938, claiming that landlords were therefore entitled to terminate leases without notice. On April 30, 1939, the law took effect. Jewish tenants and property owners were forced to leave their homes and move into buildings designated by the authorities, referred to in Nazi jargon as "Judenhäuser"(Jewish houses).

Several people were forcibly housed in Henny and Carl Möller's apartment at Rosenheimer Straße 40. In the end, there were nine of them. In the fall of 1941, Nazi authorities began systematically deporting Jews to ghettos and camps in Eastern Europe.

blocks.caption: Jews were deported not only from Germany, but from throughout EuropeImage: Scherl/SZ Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Propaganda Minister Joseph Goebbels wrote in his diary: "The main thing is that the capital of the Reich be cleansed of Jews; and I will neither rest nor relent until this goal is fully achieved." The residents of Rosenheimer Straße were among those who were subsequently deported.
Remembering at the original site

Marie Rolshoven aims to honor the fate of these individuals. In 2016, she, along with her late mother and a friend, founded the initiative Denk Mal Am Ort (a wordplay meaning both "Think about it at the site" and "Memorial at the Site") inspired by the Amsterdam project Open Jewish Homes.

blocks.caption: Marie Rolshoven (left) hosted the niece of a Jewish woman (right) who once lived in her apartment and was murdered by the NazisImage: KUBIN e.V.

blocks.text: The idea is to invite people to the very location where everyday life once occurred. "You feel a strong connection to these individuals through the actual site," says Rolshoven. "It's different from visiting a memorial."
'My brother's bed used to be right here'
Two floors below, her neighbors had a similar experience. Denk Mal Am Ort found out that the Jewish Katzenellenbogen family had previously rented the apartment.

The family escaped Nazi Germany in 1939, just in time. "In 2018, 92-year-old Joel Ludwig Katzenellenbogen was invited back here, accompanied by his daughter, son-in-law, and grandson,” Rolshoven tells DW.

The Denk Mal Am Ort initiative discovered him through Facebook. Rolshoven recounts how touched the visitors were when the former resident walked in and remarked, "Yes, I remember it clearly. My brother's bed used to be right here. He was 10 when we had to leave the country."

blocks.caption: In 2018, Joel Ludwig Katzenellenbogen (seated middle) visited the apartment where he'd spent his childhood Image: KUBIN e.V.

blocks.text: Soon there will be no eyewitnesses left

Joel Ludwig Katzenellenbogen has since passed away, along with many other eyewitnesses. This highlights the importance of intergenerational remembrance, according to Rolshoven. She has already welcomed a descendant of a former resident into her home.

Claudia Samter's mother managed to escape from Berlin to Argentina, but her aunt was not as fortunate. Seeking assistance in tracing her family's history, Claudia contacted Denk Mal Am Ort. It turned out that her aunt had once been housed in Rolshoven's apartment.

Claudia Samter has already visited twice. "After all, there's no grave in a cemetery for her to visit," says Rolshoven. "We sat at the kitchen table to talk about life today and tomorrow, and we laughed a lot and cried, too. It felt good to give this space a new purpose once again."

blocks.caption: Claudia Samter (standing right) tells 'Denk Mal Am Ort' visitors about her murdered aunt, who once lived in this apartmentImage: KUBIN e.V.

blocks.text: Denk Mal Am Ort has so far organized 90 commemorative events in eight cities this year. Many young descendants attended, according to Rolshoven. "Knowing that they had stood in this stairwell and touched the same doorknob helped them."
Seeking traces of ancestors

19-year-old Adam Ethan Klein from Switzerland also wanted to learn more about his ancestors' history. "I always knew there was a story of escape, but it was never a significant topic at home,” he says.
"They'd say, ‘Yes, your great-grandparents left Germany in 1938, just in time. Luckily, otherwise you wouldn't be here today'."

Klein says his decision to dig deeper was prompted by the spread ofantisemitism, as well as the widespread slogan "Never again is now." (Editor's note: This slogan serves as a call to actively confront antisemitism, hatred, and threats to democracy today.)

The whole family was aware of a suitcase belonging to his maternal great-grandfather in the attic. However, no one ever looked inside until Adam finally opened the suitcase and discovered dozens of documents. He also found a letter from the Hanover District Court dated June 12, 1933, addressed to his great-grandfather, attorney Max Haas.

blocks.caption: This suitcase in his grandmother's attic piqued Adam's curiosityImage: privat

blocks.text: The letter stated: "As of today, following the decree issued by the Minister of Justice, you have been removed from the list of licensed attorneys."
'They were above all one thing: Jews'

Klein was profoundly affected by the letter: "With this single sentence, it became unmistakably clear to the families that they were not quite what they had aspired to be for generations: an average German family. From that moment on, they were above all one thing: Jews."

For Klein, this was a troubling realization. So was the news that someone had stabbed an ultra-Orthodox Jew to death in Zurich while shouting antisemitic slogans. The attack occurred not far from the synagogue where he had shortly before celebrated a cousin's bar mitzvah. (Editor's note: In Judaism, a bar mitzvah is a ceremony that marks a young person's coming of age in religious matters.)

"For the first time in my life, I felt that unsettling sensation of not quite belonging. Yet Zurich is my home, the city where I've lived carefree as a Jewish Swiss from birth," Adam would later write.
"That was definitely new, uncharted territory for me. I had always thought that such things don't happen in Switzerland. Maybe that was a bit naive of me," he admits.

The subject would not let him go. Adam continued his research, determined to write his high school graduation thesis about his relatives. In the spring of 2024, he set off with his parents, sister, grandmother, uncles, aunts and several cousins to visit the places where their ancestors had lived.
A magical encounter

At some point during their journey, they found themselves in Stuttgart, standing in front of a five-story building at Hölderlinstraße 55, when a man on a bike emerged from the courtyard and approached them.

"So, are you taking a guided tour of the city, or are you planning to move here?" he asked jokingly. The man was Thomas Koch, who had spent time researching the former residents of his house. When he heard the answer, "No, we're just checking out where our ancestors lived," he was thrilled.

blocks.caption: Adam Ethan Klein (right, light pants, blue sweater) and his relatives meet Thomas Koch (center, in reflector vest)Image: privat

blocks.text: Koch had already discovered that the former owners of the house, the Merzbacher brothers, sold it in 1936 for 75,000 Reichsmarks. From that amount, they had to pay 70,000 Reichsmarks in wealth taxes and the Reich Emigration Tax. The remaining sum was just enough to cover the ship fares to Brazil and the United States.

From 1937 to 1938, a family named Hirschheimer, who worked in the plywood trade, lived on the ground floor before they were forcibly relocated to a "Judenhaus." Their trail went cold in 1939, as Koch found no further records. So, he asked, "Are you the Hirschheimer family?" They were indeed.
Koch describes the encounter as magical. Adolf and Auguste Hirschheimer were Adam's great-great-grandparents, and their daughter, Ilse, was married to Max Haas.
Adam Klein and Thomas Koch have kept in touch since then. The next time Adam visited Stuttgart, he was invited over for coffee and cake.

blocks.caption: Adolf and Auguste Hirschheimer lived with their daughter Ilse in the place where Thomas Koch now livesImage: privat

blocks.text: Adam was impressed by the beautiful apartment. "It was fascinating to imagine how my ancestors once lived there, and it probably wasn't that different. Back then, there was likely coffee and cake as well."
Adam showed Koch photos of his grandmother, Ilse, who had married at the synagogue in Stuttgart, standing in the living room in her wedding gown. "In front of the door that we still have," says Koch.

“It was really moving to discover new roommates in a historical context set in the past. And I think this experience — this process of putting myself in their shoes — is a deeply empathetic one that simply brings us together through this apartment.”
Shattered identities

Ilse and Max Haas found refuge in England, while the Hirschheimers emigrated to Switzerland in 1939. Adolf Hirschheimer died in 1940 from a heart condition, but Adam, his great-great-grandson, believes he "certainly also died of a broken heart."

blocks.caption: Thomas Koch (right) and Adam Ethan Klein have presented their joint investigation to audiences on several occasionsImage: privat

blocks.text: Auguste was brought to England by her son-in-law, Max, where the family felt homesick. "There, we were the Jews; here, we are the Germans. Try figuring that out," Ilse Haas wrote to a friend. Adam chose these lines as the title for his thesis.
Adam's great-grandparents could not find peace after being stripped of their homeland. From England, they eventually went to Israel and, at some point, returned to Europe — to Switzerland.

"At the end of their lives, my great-grandparents settled just a two-hour drive from their old homeland," Adam wrote. "When I look at their lives through the eyes of a great-grandson, it becomes clear that after breaking ties with Germany, they never managed to put down roots anywhere again."

"Remembering is important because, ultimately, we have to learn from history," says Adam. "And I think every single person has a responsibility— and the power — to actively keep memories alive. And hopefully, that can happen even without eyewitnesses.” For example, in his ancestors' former apartment.
This article was originally written in German.

articles.title: EU Commission proposes under-13s social media ban
articles.summary: Under the proposal, which will need to be negotiated with EU countries and the European Parliament in the coming months before it can become law, accounts for children between 13 and 15 will be under…

blocks.text: URSULA VON DER LEYEN. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen attends a press conference with Executive Vice-President of the European Commission for Technological Sovereignty, Security, and Democracy Henna Virkkunen (not pictured) to present the EU Kids Act, in Strasbourg, France September 17, 2026.
Yves Herman/Reuters

Under the proposal, which will need to be negotiated with EU countries and the European Parliament in the coming months before it can become law, accounts for children between 13 and 15 will be under parental control

STRASBOURG, France – European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen on Thursday, September 17, set out a sweeping plan to keep children safe from online dangers, proposing to ban under-13s from social media and require online services to design safe children’s accounts.

The move follows similar initiatives in Australia, Britain, China, India, Turkey and several EU countries underscoring rising concerns about the impact Meta’s Facebook and Instagram, TikTok, Google’s YouTube, and ChatGPT have on children’s mental health and safety.
Australia’s challenges in enforcing its world-first social media ban for children under 16 however could see Europe facing an uphill battle as well.

“Today, our children are engaging with some of the most sophisticated technology ever created, and it was not created with children’s well-being and development in mind,” von der Leyen told a press conference.
She said the proposed EU Kids Act “will set clear boundaries in the digital world just as we do it on a daily basis in the real world”.

Under the proposal, which will need to be negotiated with EU countries and the European Parliament in the coming months before it can become law, accounts for children between 13 and 15 will be under parental control.
Social media and video-sharing services, online video games, AI companions, and chatbots for children below 18 will be subject to a list of dos and don’ts.

These include a ban on addictive features, profiling-based recommender feeds, infinite scroll, reward tricks and unsolicited contact from strangers. AI companions and chatbots must be turned off by default.
Online platforms must design algorithms safe for children and provide easy-to-use parental controls and tools to block and mute users. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Philippines joins outcry over Israel's settlement plan in West Bank
articles.summary: Critics say the plan would drive a wedge through Palestinian land and threaten hopes for a Palestinian state.

blocks.text: September 17, 2026 | 5:17pm

A Palestinian boy rides his bicycle past Israeli armoured vehicles deployed at the entrance to al-Ain camp for Palestinian refugees, west of Nablus in the Israeli-occupied West Bank on September 17, 2026, during an Israeli military raid.
AFP / Zain Jaafar
MANILA, Philippines – The Philippines has joined a growing number of governments raising alarm over Israel's renewed push to kickstart its E1 settlement plan in the occupied West Bank.

The Department of Foreign Affairs (DFA) said on Thursday, September 17, that it noted "with alarm" Israel's efforts to advance its E1 (East 1) settlement plan – long condemned internationally – and "the continued rise of settler violence in the West Bank."
It warned that these actions "may contravene international law" and harm efforts to reach "a just, lasting and comprehensive solution to the Middle East conflict."
The DFA statement comes a month after Israel opened bidding for 1,234 homes in the area of the E1 settlement project.
The United Nations and international rights watchdog Human Rights Watch have flagged how settler attacks on Palestinians are at their highest and most serious on record.
E1 is a largely undeveloped stretch of land between Jerusalem and the Israeli settlement of Ma'aleh Adumim.

While there are already thousands of Israeli settlers in the occupied West Bank, critics say the E1 plan would break the link between the northern and southern West Bank and further cut off east Jerusalem from nearby Palestinian communities.
The project, according to Israeli Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich, will aid Israel in preventing the creation of a Palestinian state, the Jerusalem Post reported.
The DFA urged "all parties" to stop unilateral actions that "erode the conditions for peace and undermine the viability of a future Palestinian state."
It said the Philippines remains firm in upholding Palestinians' rights, particularly their right to self-determination.

Manila's statement follows a joint statement by 22 countries, released on August 20, calling Israel's decision to publish E1 construction tenders "unacceptable." Among nations that signed the joint statement are the United Kingdom, France, Germany, Canada and Australia.
The signatories said international law is clear that Israeli settlements in the West Bank are illegal, a position they said the UN Security Council has reaffirmed.

More Palestinians were forcibly displaced by settler attacks, demolitions and evictions in the first four months of 2026 than in all of 2025, according to the United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs.
The Fourth Geneva Convention bars an occupying power from forcibly transferring people out of occupied territory and from moving its own civilians into it.

articles.title: Iran school bombing: grounds to believe US was behind atrocity, UN finds
articles.summary:
Fact-finding mission says military strikes on school and sports facility in ⁠February constitute war ⁠crimes

A UN fact-finding mission on Iran has said there are reasonable grounds to…

blocks.text: A UN fact-finding mission on Iran has said there are reasonable grounds to believe the US was behind two military strikes on a school and sports facility in Iran in ⁠February, and that these constituted war ⁠crimes.
It also found Iranian ​authorities committed crimes against humanity during their deadly crackdown on anti-government protests.

The findings by the independent international fact-finding mission on Iran, to be submitted to the UN human rights council in Geneva, examined the ⁠US’s conduct during the Iran war that began in February and the Iranian government’s response to nationwide unrest that begun in late December.
US officials have previously said military ⁠operations are conducted in accordance with the law of armed conflict, while Iran has consistently rejected allegations of systematic rights violations.

The UN experts said they found ​reasonable grounds to believe US forces were responsible for an attack on the ‌Shajareh Tayyebeh primary school in the city of ‌Minab, where more than 150 people were killed, including around 120 schoolchildren, according to Iranian officials.
It constituted an indiscriminate attack causing civilian deaths and damage to ‌civilian infrastructure, amounting to a war crime under international law, the mission concluded.

blocks.caption: A rubble-strewn classroom at Shajareh Tayyebeh school. Photograph: Vahid Salemi/AP

blocks.text: According to the report, the US relied on intelligence suggesting a senior Iranian military commander was present at the site but failed to adequately verify the information before launching the strike. Investigators said the failure to update targeting intelligence and confirm the building was a military objective amounted to more than mere negligence.

“Rather, the US directed the strikes at the building of the school while being aware of a substantial risk of striking a civilian object and acting recklessly as regards the possibility that this would happen.”

In June the US president, Donald Trump, said ‌that “nobody” purposefully attacked a girls’ school in Iran in February, citing an investigation into the incident. Reuters first reported that an initial internal US military investigation showed US forces were probably responsible for the fatal strike in Minab in southern Iran.
The Pentagon has since elevated ​the inquiry but it has not published any preliminary findings.
UN experts said the school was a clearly identifiable civilian object and found no evidence it was being used for military purposes.

The experts reached a similar conclusion over a strike on a sports centre in Lamerd. The report said the attack damaged nearby residential buildings and a school and killed and injured 22 civilians. It concluded that the strike was indiscriminate and therefore constituted a war crime.
US Central Command said in a statement in March that ⁠US forces did not launch any strikes into the city of Lamerd on that day.

The UN mission found ​that the Iranian authorities carried out a widespread and systematic ​attack against civilians during protests that erupted in late ​December last year, involving unlawful killings, torture, arbitrary detention, enforced disappearances and severe restrictions on freedom of expression.

Rights groups say bystanders were among ​those killed during the biggest crackdown ‌since Shia Muslim clerics took ​power in the 1979 revolution. Tehran blamed “terrorists ​and rioters” backed by exiled opponents and foreign foes the US and Israel.

The investigation said it could not independently verify the death toll, but that it believed the number of dead and injured was probably far higher than official figures, which say 3,038 people were killed and 25,000 people injured.

The government’s response to the protests, including violence and killings, cutting off the internet and use of the death penalty, marked a significant escalation from previous patterns of suppressing dissent, the report said.

articles.title: NEA seeks extra P7 billion to eliminate non-technical system losses
articles.summary: NEA says eliminating non-technical system losses will require a phased transition, with cooperatives needing billions in loans for metering and other upgrades before they can absorb the costs

blocks.text: Electric company contractors install wires for newly installed electric meters on a utility pole along Jose Abad Santos Avenue in Manila on September 3, 2026.
Rappler
NEA says eliminating non-technical system losses will require a phased transition, with cooperatives needing billions in loans for metering and other upgrades before they can absorb the costs

items: The National Electrification Administration (NEA) is requesting an additional P7 billion from Congress to help electric cooperatives address non-technical system losses, which is more than its proposed P6.49-billion budget for 2027.

The P7 billion is not part of the National Expenditure Program and aims to support electric cooperatives in eliminating costs associated with unaccounted electricity due to issues like theft and inaccurate meters.

NEA's proposed budget includes P850 million for loans to cooperatives, but additional funding is necessary to implement a four-stage program aimed at reducing non-technical losses, which could financially impact many cooperatives if not addressed.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

MANILA, Philippines – The National Electrification Administration (NEA) is asking Congress for an additional P7 billion to help electric cooperatives eliminate non-technical system losses, an amount larger than the agency’s entire P6.49-billion proposed budget for 2027.

The P7 billion is not included in the National Expenditure Program (NEP) submitted by the executive branch to Congress. Under the proposed 2027 budget, NEA only has P850 million in national-government equity earmarked as loans to electric cooperatives, alongside P5.64 billion in subsidies and other funding under its National Rural Electrification Program.

NEA Administrator Antonio Mariano Almeda told senators during deliberations on the Department of Energy’s proposed 2027 budget that the agency is now seeking the P7 billion in addition to its existing loan equity fund to cushion electric cooperatives from the financial impact of removing non-technical system losses from consumers’ electricity bills.
“The P7 billion is a fund in addition to the loan equity fund of the National Electrification Administration to loan to the electric cooperatives,” Almeda said on Thursday, September 17.

Under NEA’s proposed 2027 budget, the P850-million equity infusion is already intended to finance loans to electric cooperatives. The agency targets facilitating P850 million worth of loans to 18 cooperatives next year, up from P810 million targeted in 2026.
There is no separate allocation in the NEP for system loss reduction.

Non-technical system losses refer to electricity that goes unaccounted for because of factors such as pilferage, illegal connections, and inaccurate or missing meters. They differ from technical losses, which naturally occur as electricity travels through distribution lines and cannot be completely eliminated.

System loss has become a hot policy issue after President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. used his July State of the Nation Address to call for an immediate amendment of the Electric Power Industry Reform Act in order to prohibit utilities from passing system loss charges, including the corresponding VAT, on to consumers.

The directive has put pressure on energy agencies and regulators to work out how those charges can be reduced or removed without undermining the finances and operations of electric cooperatives and other distribution utilities.

blocks.caption: Meralco chair Pangilinan: Power industry ‘may not survive’ if asked to absorb system loss

blocks.text: Almeda said electric cooperatives would have to spend heavily on metering as the government moves to stop passing non-technical losses on to consumers, including installing meters for currently unmetered connections and replacing meters as authorities crack down on electricity theft.

NEA estimates its four-stage program would require around P7.5 billion in capital expenditures. Almeda said the first phase, which would reduce non-technical system losses to 25%, would require around P4 billion. Another P1 billion would be needed for each of the next two stages, followed by P1.5 billion for complete elimination.
The proposed assistance would not be a subsidy. Instead, NEA would lend the money to electric cooperatives for investments needed to reduce their losses.

At an earlier DOE press conference, Almeda said NEA estimated that 62 of the country’s 121 electric cooperatives could suffer financial losses if 25% of non-technical system losses could no longer be recovered from consumers.

Almeda has pointed to the Zamboanga City Electric Cooperative as an example of what the program could achieve. He said its system loss rate fell from around 20% in January 2026 to roughly 13% by July following interventions that included additional metering, capital infusion, and management measures. – Rappler.com

blocks.text: Published September 17, 2026 5:04pm

Following a consultation with amici curiae or friends of the court, the senator-judges will have a meeting regarding the voting threshold needed to either convict or acquit Vice President Sara Duterte in her impeachment trial.
In a Super Radyo dzBB report from Nimfa Ravelo on Thursday, Senate President Pro Tempore Vicente Sotto III said that they will have a caucus on the matter but is unsure when this will take place.

Mga senador, pagpupulungan ang voting threshold o pagbilang sa boto para sa pag-convict o pag-acquit kay Vice Pres. Sara Duterte na kanilang nililitis bilang Impeachment Court. | via @nimfaravelo https://t.co/WTxPtMxVO7— DZBB Super Radyo (@dzbb) September 17, 2026
Meanwhile, Senate Deputy Majority Leader JV Ejercito said the caucus might take place on Monday, where they may reach a consensus.

The senator-judges had asked the former justices for their insights on whether the senators that are detained, on the run and those abroad should be included in the voting to impeach or acquit Duterte.
For Ejercito, it was important that senator-judges attended the proceedings so that they could render a fair decision, rather than relying on transcripts and recordings.
Senate impeachment presiding officer Francis Escudero had initially ruled that 16 votes were required to convict Duterte, which is two-thirds of the entire 24 senators.

articles.title: River home to 500 crocodiles chosen as Olympic rowing venue
articles.summary: A river that is home to about 500 saltwater crocodiles is given the OK to host Olympic and Paralympic rowing and canoeing events at the 2032 Brisbane Games.

blocks.text: A river that is home to about 500 saltwater crocodiles has been given the OK to host Olympic and Paralympic rowing and canoeing events at the 2032 Brisbane Games.
The course on the Fitzroy River in Rockhampton, Queensland, has passed an independent technical assessment into its suitability.

The assessment did not consider the crocodiles but instead looked at "how the course would perform under a range of conditions, weather patterns, water levels and flood risk at both Games time and throughout the period leading into the Games".

The report was commissioned by the Games Independent Infrastructure and Coordination Authority (GIICA), which noted, external that the Fitzroy River Flatwater Facility "is already a training and competition venue for flatwater sports, supporting school state championships, local regattas, and national team training camps".
World Rowing and Paddle Worldwide, formerly International Canoe Federation, both endorsed the course.

"Based on the extensive analysis undertaken, we now know that the Fitzroy River is capable of providing fair competition conditions during the period of the Games, consistent with the requirements of Olympic and Paralympic Rowing," World Rowing President Jean-Christophe Rolland said., external

Paddle Worldwide President Thomas Konietzko said: "The quality and depth of the technical work undertaken has significantly improved our understanding of the field of play and provides confidence to us and our athletes that the course can deliver fair competition for Canoe Sprint athletes."
Brisbane 2032 President Andrew Liveris played down the issue of crocodiles last year.
"There are sharks in the ocean and we're still surfing... it's a can do, not a can't do - please change the mindset here," he said at the time.

Speaking on Thursday about the venue having now been given the go-ahead, he said: "The endorsement provides additional certainty as we move into the next phase of venue planning and Games delivery, ensuring all future design and operational work continues to focus solely on Rockhampton."
Saltwater crocodiles - known locally as Salties - live in both freshwater and saltwater and can grow to be in excess of six metres long.

articles.title: Fiji declares HIV a national crisis, 1 in 60 adults carry it
articles.summary: Fiji's government estimates that HIV prevalence has almost tripled in the last five years. It's expanding testing, prevention and treatment services. In 2025 the tiny island recorded 16 times more…

image.caption: Fiji's government said that two in every 100 pregnant women were living with HIV [FILE: April 20, 2026]Image: AFP

blocks.text: Fiji has declared HIV a national health crisis, pledging a "whole-of-government response to address the significant rise in HIV cases and protect communities across the country."

The Pacific island's government announced the move earlier this week, saying it had recorded 2,016 new HIV diagnoses in 2025 — 16 times the number recorded in 2019. The figures point to the virus spreading beyond high-risk groups like drug users and sex workers into the wider population.
Fiji said the known adult prevalence of the virus had almost tripled in five years in the country of a little more than 900,000 people.

blocks.caption: The government is trying to boost free outreach and testing programsImage: AFP

blocks.text: What did Fiji's government say about HIV and its response?
"An estimated one in every 60 adults is now living with HIV, compared with one in 167 five years ago," the government said.
"Among pregnant women, two in every 100 are living with HIV, while 59 babies were born with HIV in 2025, with 18 dying before their first birthday," it warned.

However, the government also said that expanded testing was helping health services reach more people and identify cases that might have previously gone undetected, noting a period of slower surveillance starting around a decade ago.
Health Minister Ratu Atonio Lalabalavu and four other revlevant Cabinet ministers would form a sub-committe to "help remove barriers to rapid action."

blocks.caption: The UN estimates that fewer than half of Fiji's HIV sufferers know their status, at least as of last year prior to the current efforts to boost screening servicesImage: AFP

blocks.text: The administration based in the capital and port city Suva said it was expanding access to free HIV testing, prevention services and treatment — including rapid testing, prevention medecine for people at high risk, harm-reduction measures for people who inject drugs and free treatment for diagnosed HIV sufferers.

"The response is focused on protecting lives, improving access to health services and reducing stigma," the government said. "Fiji is also receiving support from international partners, including Australia, New Zealand, India, the Global Fund and the United Nations."
It reminded people that testing was free and confidential across the country, saying "knowing your HIV status allows you to take informed steps to protect your health and others."
UNAIDS welcomes response, estimates less than half of Fiji's HIV sufferers know their status
UNAIDS in Geneva responded to the move on Wednesday, welcoming Fiji's decision to accelerate its response.

"Fiji has recognized the urgency of the moment and is stepping up its response," said UNAIDS Executive Director Winnie Byanyima. "It is also a stark reminder to the world that AIDS is not over. HIV epidemics can change quickly, and countries need health and community systems that are ready to respond urgently."
The UN organization said that among Fijian cases with a known mode of transmission, more than half were linked to sexual transmission and more than 42% to injecting drug use.

UNAIDS estimated that new infections increased 12-fold between 2010 and 2025 in Fiji. It also said that of an estimated 9,100 people living with the virus in 2025, "only 39% knew their HIV status and just 22% were accessing antiretroviral treatment."
However, giving medical advances in recent years and increased efficacy of treatments, it said that there was time to turn the tide.

"The national crisis declaration is a call for action, not fear. HIV is not transmitted through everyday contact, and people on effective treatment with an undetectable viral load do not sexually transmit HIV," said UNAIDS' Eamonn Murphy. "Fiji still has an opportunity to change the course of this epidemic."

The country director for Fiji at UNAIDS, Renata Ram, told the AFP news agency that transmission rates started rising around 2019 when a group of "very high-risk" injecting drug users emerged, primarily in the sex worker community.

Pacific islands like Fiji have become transit hubs for drugs from Latin America and Asia destined for the lucrative markets in Australia and New Zealand. This has also led to increased drug use on the islands themselves, often as a result of foreign crime syndicates paying their local associates with product.

articles.title: Senators react to Rodrigo Duterte's first in-person appearance before ICC
articles.summary: Some senators on Thursday shared their reactions after former president Rodrigo Duterte made his first in-person appearance before the International Criminal Court.

blocks.text: Published September 17, 2026 5:02pm
Some senators on Thursday shared their reactions after former president Rodrigo Duterte made his first in-person appearance before the International Criminal Court.
Senator JV Ejercito told reporters that he felt sad seeing Duterte, whom he described as “very frail.”

“May lungkot akong naramdaman nung nakita ko siya for the first time in a long time na siyempre parang buto’t balat na eh. Napakapayat, very frail, ang haba ng buhok… I have to admit, may kalungkutan akong naramdaman nung nakita ko siya,” Ejercito said.
(I felt sad when I saw him for the first time in a long time because he is very thin and very frail, with his hair grown long. I have to admit, I felt a sense of sadness when I saw him.)
When asked for a comment on the reaction of families of victims of the Duterte administration’s war on drugs, the senator said, "Let justice take its course.”

“Let justice take its course kung saan hahantong ito. Kaya lang, sa akin kasi history will be the final judge. Para sa akin kahit sino, kahit sinong presidente… Hindi tayo Diyos para humusga,” Ejercito said.
(Let justice take its course and see where it leads. But for me, history will be the final judge. As far as I’m concerned, whoever it may be, even any president, we are not God to pass judgment.)

Dressed in a black jacket and white button-down polo, Duterte attended the third status conference in his crimes against humanity case as part of preparations for his trial, which is set to begin on November 30.
Meanwhile, Senator Bong Go, a long-time aide of Duterte, posted a photo of the former president with the caption “Tatay Digong” and a green heart emoji.
Duterte ally Senator Robin Padilla said he is happy to see the former president but sad at the thought of his condition in the detention facility.

“Ako po ay nabigla at hindi inaasahan na tulo ang luha sa tuwa at nakita na siya ngunit binalot ng lungkot dahil batid ko na malakas lang ang loob ni Tatay Digong. Kaya ng tapang at malasakit pero hindi na kaya ng 81 years old niyang katawan ang kulungan,” Padilla said.

(I was caught off guard and tears of joy fell when I saw him. But I am also sad because I know that Tatay Digong is strong-willed. He has courage and compassion, but his 81-year-old body can no longer endure being in prison.)
Senator Rodante Marcoleta, another ally of the Dutertes, said he was happy to see the former president in good condition.
“Nakita ko na siya na maganda ang kaniyang kalayagan kung titingnan mo ang kaniyang mukha. I am happy for him,” Marcoleta said.
(I saw that he was in good condition, judging from his appearance. I am happy for him.)
Unlike the previous two hearings, Duterte did not waive his appearance.
“This is the first time that Mr. Duterte has been in this court. As far as the trial chamber is concerned, if he wishes to leave for any reason, he may do so,” Presiding Judge Joanna Korner said.
Duterte was arrested and taken to The Hague on March 12, 2025. He last appeared before the ICC via video link on March 14, 2025.—AOL, GMA News

articles.title: Toronto cop charged in Project South allegedly didn't care if selling information harmed people
articles.summary: Toronto police Const. Timothy Barnhardt knew the information he sold to a civilian from police database searches could help facilitate "serious violence and explicitly stated that he did not care if…

image.caption: Brian Da Costa is one of four civilians charged in Project South who investigators connected to Toronto South Detention Centre inmate Gurpreet Singh, according to the ITO. (Pam Davies/CBC)

blocks.text: Toronto·CBC Investigates

Toronto police Const. Timothy Barnhardt knew the information he sold to a civilian from police database searches could help facilitate "serious violence and explicitly stated that he did not care if individuals were harmed," according to newly reportable details from an Information to Obtain application supporting more than 50 warrants in the Project South investigation.
Investigators believe inmate connected to 4 charged in probe ordered alleged hit on corrections official: ITO
· CBC News
· Posted: Sep 17, 2026 5:00 AM EDT | Last Updated: 30 minutes ago
Cop charged in Project South didn’t care if people were hurt after selling information: court docs

Toronto police Const. Timothy Barnhardt knew the information he sold to a civilian from police database searches could help facilitate "serious violence and explicitly stated that he did not care if individuals were harmed," according to an Information to Obtain (ITO) application supporting more than 50 warrants in the Project South investigation.
The sweeping corruption probe began in June 2025, when York Regional Police thwarted an alleged plot to kill a senior corrections official from Toronto South Detention Centre (TSDC).

Investigators subsequently discovered Barnhardt allegedly ran an unauthorized search on the official's licence plate less than a month before the attempted hit, and he is accused of then sharing confidential information about that official with civilian Brian Da Costa. The identity of the senior corrections official is covered by a publication ban for their safety.

items: Inmate and jail guard investigated, but not charged in Project South alleged murder plot

blocks.text: Both Barnhardt and Da Costa are in custody facing several charges in the probe, which have not been tested in court. Their lawyers declined to comment for this story.

The unauthorized query on the jail official was one of 17 times Barnhardt allegedly accessed the Ministry of Transportation server to do searches while off-duty in the first six months of last year, according to the ITO. Police-intercepted communications revealed to investigators that Barnhardt "routinely sold confidential database information to known criminal associate Da Costa, often at Da Costa's direction."
A publication ban was lifted on those revelations, and many others, from the Project South ITO on Wednesday in a ruling from Ontario Superior Court Justice Laura Bird.

Other new details include why investigators believed TSDC inmate Gurpreet Singh ordered the hit on the senior jail official, along with his alleged connections to a corrections officer and four men charged in Project South, including Da Costa.
Neither Singh nor the corrections officer have been charged in this investigation.

CBC News was part of a group of media organizations fighting to lift a publication ban on the ITO in court. Bird previously lifted the ban on some details earlier this summer. In her decision this week, Bird lifted the ban on the majority of the rest of the court record.

"Permitting the media to publish the vast majority of the ITO while maintaining a temporary publication ban over limited portions of it strikes an appropriate balance between the court openness principle and the fair trial rights of the criminal defendants," wrote Bird.

An ITO is a legal document from a police officer laying out the evidence they have of a criminal offence in order to request judicial authorization for a warrant or production order from a judge or justice of the peace. The allegations in the ITO have not been tested in court.

The search warrants were executed as investigators arrested and charged seven Toronto police officers, one retired cop and 19 civilians in Project South. The charge against one of those civilians has since been stayed, and one of the officers retired and pleaded guilty to two charges in July.
The charges against the others accused in Project South have not yet been tested in court.
Police believed Singh behind attempted hit: ITO

Elsewhere in the ITO, police say Singh had motive to harm the senior corrections official who was targeted, and that he was named by that official as one of a handful of inmates who'd expressed hostility toward them. The official told police that Singh and his former cellmate were angry after the official seized cellphones and steroids from their cell and then separated the pair.
CBC News previously reported that Singh and correctional officer Nishwant Dosanjh were investigated for potential involvement in the alleged conspiracy.

The ITO also states Dosanjh was Singh's former romantic partner and she allegedly took the photo of the senior corrections official's licence plate in the employee area of the jail. The photo was allegedly later provided to Da Costa and then shared with Barnhardt, who's accused of using the image to search a police database on May 27, 2025.
The results of that query were allegedly provided to Da Costa, then shared with a gun-for-hire group accused of conspiring to kill the senior corrections official the following month.
The allegations in the ITO concerning Dosanjh and Singh have not led to charges, nor have they been tested in court.

In a statement, Dosanjh’s lawyer, Kim Schofield, told CBC News her client has co-operated with police, maintains her innocence and had no part in the attempt on the senior corrections official's life.

Schofield says she hired an independent digital forensics expert to review the "data dump" she received of Dosanjh's seized cell phone. The lawyer says the expert found no photos or chat discussions relating to the attempted hit.
"There is absolutely nothing to connect her to that incident," wrote Schofield.

CBC News contacted Singh's lawyer for comment, but did not receive a response before publication. In an emailed statement in June, Singh's lawyer, Brian Greenspan, said his client had not been charged with any offence in Canada, months after the execution of the February warrants.

Singh has been held at the Toronto jail since his October 2024 arrest amid allegations he acted as an accomplice in a drug-smuggling organization allegedly involving killings and led by accused cocaine kingpin Ryan Wedding.
Singh is fighting extradition to California.
Inmate connected to 4 men charged in Project South: ITO

Investigators also connected Singh with others charged in Project South. According to the ITO, Singh was associated with four of the civilians charged in the corruption probe, including Elwyn Satanowsky, Da Costa and Dequon Lemonious.

Satanowsky is accused of arranging several shootings connected with the probe. He deposited money into Singh's inmate trust account and he spoke to Singh on the phone more than 300 times between the beginning of January and mid-September 2025, according to the ITO.
Police intercepted communications between Da Costa and Singh through TSDC's inmate telephone system.
Lemonious is charged with conspiracy to murder the senior corrections official. The ITO identifies him as someone "who plans and structures violent criminal activity" within a gunmen-for-hire group.

In an intercepted phone call, Keajean Doman, an alleged enforcer in the group also charged in the conspiracy, blames Lemonious for "plays" that resulted in his incarceration. Doman was arrested last September after allegedly carrying out a shooting related to Project South in Vaughan, Ont.
Other intercepts connect Singh and Lemonious by way of them both speaking to, or about, a former cellmate of Singh's who's in custody on a different range at TSDC, according to the ITO.
CBC News contacted lawyers for Satanowsky and Lemonious for this story but neither provided a comment before publication.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Nicole Brockbank is a reporter for CBC Toronto's Enterprise Unit. She digs up, researches and reports GTA-focused investigative and enterprise stories. nicole.brockbank@cbc.ca

articles.title: Jürgen Klopp's first Germany squad includes 44 players
articles.summary: Germany's new head coach Jürgen Klopp has named a huge squad for his first four games, splitting them into two groups. A host of new faces is included.

image.caption: Jürgen Klopp announced an XXL squad for his first games in chargeImage: John Macdougall/AFP

blocks.text: Jürgen Klopp's Germany era has begun as the new head coach announced his first squad on Thursday.

To manage the newly organized international break that sees the September and October pauses merged into one, Klopp selected 44 players splitting them into two squads across the four games. Klopp did add though, that Nico Schlotterbeck, Jamal Musiala and Serge Gnabry might stay for the whole two weeks. Goalkeeper Finn Dahmen is also in both squads as Klopp wants to take a closer look at him.
"It's unusual to have four games in two weeks," said Klopp at the press conference.
"I want to get to know as many players as possible. There is no A or B team. The squads are put together in a way that makes sense on the pitch and in terms of character and experience.
"There are few names here that will surprise, but we wanted it to be a part of their development," he added.
"We didn't look at what we were missing but rather what we have and realized how much football talent we have."

There were a total of 11 new players included, with the biggest surprise being Hoffenheim's Bambase Conte, Stuttgart defender Finn Jeltsch, Celtic's Mika Baur, and Freiburg's Derry Scherhant. Younes Ebnoutalib (23), Frankfurt's breakout forward was included, with Klopp saying he was a "huge talent" who was "hugely delighted" to be included.

Felix Keidel, the 23-year-old midfielder from Elversberg who has played just three Bundesliga games was another big surprise. Keidel can also play at right back, but has been predominately used as a holding midfielder since the small-town team won promotion to the top flight.
Oliver Baumann, Deniz Undav and Leroy Sane were not included.
Politically, Klopp wants to win back the flag

Klopp spoke at length on many subjects, saying he wanted more from his players, that how the team played was more important than who played, and that his whole career had prepared him for this job. He also spoke on what it means to be German in the modern political and social climate.

"I hope that I don't have to talk about politics in future press conferences but from my sporting perspective, I would like to win back the flag. I don't want national pride to be left to the wrong people. I am so proud to do this job and we are a wonderful country," Klopp said.

"It, this team and sport, is here to make us feel better and to develop a sense of togetherness and feel the power of sport," he said, citing Zverev's recent success in tennis and the basketball World Cup. "We are responsible for creating this atmosphere."
ter Stegen one of many old faces who return to Germany squad

Marc-Andre ter Stegen returns to the Germany squad after a lengthy injury layoff, and Klopp called him the number one at the moment. The 33-year-old goalkeeper, who is now playing his club football at Ajax, last appeared for Germany in the Nations League Finals last summer.
"I've known Marc-Andre for a long time," Klopp said.
"He has the right amount of experience. He is a keeper that can play with the ball and he is also an excellent shot-stopper. Everything depends on performance."

Said El Mala was included. The Cologne youngster was a surprise inclusion in Germany's World Cup qualifying campaign in November 2025, but didn't make an appearance. He is widely expected to be one of the faces of this new Germany team under Klopp.
Notable absences in this first Germany squad under the new boss were Deniz Undav, Leroy Sane and Oliver Baumann.

Germany's international break starts in Amsterdam against the Netherlands on September 24, before a home game in Augsburg against Greece three days later. On October 1, Germany are to play Serbia in Munich before traveling to Thessaloniki to play Greece in the final game of the international break on October 4.

articles.title: One dead after torrential rain and flash floods hit Barcelona region
articles.summary: Flooding has caused widespread disruption across Valencia and Catalonia in north-east Spain.

blocks.text: North-eastern Spain has been hit by torrential rain and flash floods, leaving one person dead and causing widespread disruption across the region.
Spain's national weather agency AEMET issued warnings for heavy rain across eastern regions on Wednesday, including a red alert for Barcelona's coastline.
Rescuers recovered the body of a man on Thursday in Olivella, around 40km (25 miles) west of Barcelona, after his car was swept away by a stream, authorities said.

The deluge has disrupted travel across Catalonia and Valencia, with flights cancelled and roads submerged. Authorities have advised against unnecessary travel, while Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez warned of "very complicated situations".
Emergency services in Catalonia said they received more than 850 calls related to the downpours and catalogued over 500 incidents.
Catalan firefighters said on X on Thursday that they had recovered the "lifeless body of a man" in Olivella, correcting earlier reports that had identified the missing person as a woman.
Videos shared on social media showed partially submerged cars and rescue workers attempting to reach a vehicle trapped in a heavily flooded underpass.
In Barcelona, some metro stations were closed and buses diverted, while regional trains were disrupted and flights delayed or cancelled at El Prat airport.
Neighbouring Valencia had more than 70mm (2.76in) of rain fall in just half an hour in several municipalities, according to AVAMET.
"Rarely have we seen such rainfall accumulations in 30 minutes," the meteorological association said on X.
Emergency services reported 478 incidents in the Valencia province, mostly involving property damage, leaks and traffic disruption.
In the regional capital, all metro lines were suspended and the city's airport shuttered for several hours, causing flights to be diverted.

articles.title: Australia to restrict student, backpacker visas in migration clampdown
articles.summary: The Australian interior minister said reducing migration is needed to address housing pressures. The move comes amid a far-right surge in the polls.

image.caption: Burke denied the move was a response to pressure from the far-rightImage: via REUTERS

blocks.text: Australia will cut migration by toughening visa rules for foreign students, backpackers, and working holiday-makers, the Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke said Thursday.

Under the new rules, foreign students will no longer be allowed to bring partners and children to join them while they study in Australia, while people who overstay their working holiday visas will face tougher enforcement.
The government is also cracking down on so-called "visa hopping," where foreign migrants who are already in Australia move from one type of temporary visa to another to extend their stay.

"If you want to come on a temporary basis to Australia, apply for a temporary visa. If you want ‌to ​come to Australia permanently, apply for a permanent visa. And if you no longer have a valid visa, you should leave Australia," Burke said.
What else did the Home Affairs Minister say about the migration reforms?

In remarks to the National Press Club in Canberra on Thursday, Burke insisted that immigration remains "fundamentally a strength" for Australia, but acknowledged that rules needed adjusting to ease pressure on housing.
"We need immigration to soften enough that housing has a chance to catch up," he said, while stressing the housing shortage was not caused by migrants.
Burke said it was "simply demonstrably wrong" that his ruling center-left Labor party was beefing up its visa rules as a response to a surge in the polls by the far-right One Nation.

This year, the group has become one of the country's most popular parties, campaigning on pledges to slash migration to the country as part of its "Australia First" approach, which has drawn similarities to US President Donald Trump.
The hard-right party said this week that it would cut the number of temporary migrants by 750,000 over the next three years to give Australians "breathing space."
The cost of living and immigration have ranked as some of voters' most pressing concerns in recent polls.
How this far-right outsider is winning in Australia
What is the migration situation in Australia?
The changes are set to see net annual migration fall from the current 300,000 to around 225,000 by 2028. That would see numbers return to the levels before the Covid-19 pandemic.
Annual migration surged to its highest level of 538,000 in 2022, after borders reopened.
Data on Thursday showed that migration numbers had declined to 292,100 in the year to March, 47% below the peak following the pandemic, Burke said.
Students make up the biggest immigrant group: some 753,000 foreign students live in Australia, most of whom come from China and India.
The reforms will see Australia return to its policy of a decade earlier when those who overstayed were given two weeks to leave the country or face detention and deportation, the minister said.
People seeking to extend their working holiday visas in rural areas will enter a ballot for a second or third year.
Applicants with skills in construction and housing will be prioritized for visas, Burke said.
Relatives of visa holders wanting to visit the country will have "no further stay" conditions applied to their visas.

articles.title: Mr. Big stings are inadmissible by default. Here's why Dean Penney's was allowed at trial
articles.summary: Perhaps the biggest decision in the Dean Penney trial happened before the jury was even selected. Here's why a judge allowed the jury to hear evidence from the RCMP's covert operation commonly known…

image.caption: Dean Penney was sentenced to life in prison without the possibility of parole for 25 years for the first-degree murder of his estranged wife, Jennifer Hillier-Penney. He was arrested following a pair of confessions to an undercover police officer posing as the leader of a criminal organization. (Rya

blocks.text: In a murder case with no body and very little physical evidence, Dean Penney's admissions to an undercover RCMP officer posing as a crime boss were everything.

Penney confessed twice to killing his estranged wife, Jennifer Hillier-Penney, and disposing of her body in the ocean near his cabin. The videos were damning — some jurors appeared shaken as family members wept in the courtroom.
But it was never guaranteed the jury would hear the videotaped confessions.

items: As Dean Penney gets life sentence, sister says she's 'lost' without Jennifer Hillier-Penney
Dean Penney found guilty of first-degree murder

blocks.text: The RCMP used a covert tactic known as a Mr. Big sting, in which police get close to a suspect and invite them into a fictitious criminal organization. The operation ends in an interview with the head of the organization, who attempts to elicit a confession.

Mr. Big stings are presumptively inadmissible in Canadian law. Before a trial begins, the Crown must establish the probative value — how the confessions help establish the truth of an allegation — outweighs the prejudicial effect of the operation.
Justice Vikas Khaladkar published his pre-trial decision on Wednesday, showing why he allowed the confessions to be played for the jury.
The rules on Mr. Big stings were largely established by the Supreme Court of Canada in the 2014 case of a Newfoundland man accused of killing his daughters near Gander.
The top court found the RCMP ran afoul of Nelson Hart's rights on several fronts in that investigation, resulting in a framework for how Mr. Big operations should be handled by courts in the future.
Khaladkar said he had to consider seven aspects of how the confession was obtained.
1. Length of the operation
The covert investigation into Dean Penney lasted more than four years.
"On its face, that is a lengthy period," Khaladkar wrote. "However, the evidence presented explains much of the delay."
Penney was a fisherman and told his contacts within the fictitious criminal organization that he would be unavailable during the fishing season.

The COVID-19 pandemic also played a significant role. The undercover operators testified at trial about concerns they could inadvertently bring the virus to the small community, especially given the age of Penney's parents at the time.
There was also a stretch where Penney had changed his phone number and couldn't be reached.
2. Number of interactions
There were 71 documented scenarios over the course of those four years.

Over the span of the investigation, the scenarios varied greatly — from snowmobiling and watching movies at Penney's cabin, to smuggling weapons off a military base and stealing fuel near the U.S. border in Alberta.

"When one looks not simply at the passage of time, but at the actual number and nature of the interactions, I am not persuaded that either the length of the operation or the number of scenarios undermines the reliability of the confession," Khaladkar wrote.
3. Nature of the relationship that developed
Khaladkar had to examine Penney's relationships with all the undercover operators, but one in particular deserved closer attention.

An officer who went by the pseudonym Vic ingratiated himself with Penney far more than the others. Testimony at trial showed Vic became Penney's best friend — to the point where Vic told the court he hoped the investigation would have proved Penney was innocent.

But Khaladkar said Penney's situation was much different than the one presented in the Nelson Hart case, where the accused was "socially isolated and highly vulnerable to the relationships created by the operation."

"Mr. Penney had existing social and familial ties in the community, and those relationships remained intact during much of the operation," Khaladkar wrote. "In particular, he had the support of his mother while she was alive, and he continued to have the support of his father, with whom he shared his fishing earnings."

Penney also still had a relationship with his youngest daughter, Deana, and was living with a girlfriend at the time of the investigation. A pre-sentence report conducted before Penney's sentencing said the couple has since gotten engaged.
4. Inducements offered
Penney was paid about $27,000 in total over the 71 scenarios across four years of the operation.

At the time of the confessions in 2023, Penney had fallen on hard times. The family fishing business suffered after the death of his mother, and his father's failing health meant he could no longer work.
"Even so, I do not find that he was destitute or without alternatives," Khaladkar said, noting he still had two properties and a number of vehicles he could have sold.

"In my view, the money paid over time was not particularly significant. Certainly, it was not sufficient to be coercive or overwhelming," the judge continued. "I do not doubt that he had a cash-flow problem. However, I am not persuaded that his financial circumstances were so desperate as to make a false confession reasonably likely."
5. Presence or absence of threats
Khaladkar said Penney did not experience any threats during the course of the Mr. Big operation.

He said he was satisfied there was evidence that the undercover officers "took care not to suggest that the accused would suffer physical harm if he withdrew from the organization or declined to continue."

The undercover officers told the court several times how they always offered Penney an exit ramp before a scenario. They said he could have left the organization at any time, but he chose to stay involved.
6. Conduct of the interrogation

Leading up to the interrogation, Penney had been told another member of the organization, Ryan — who was said to be terminally ill — was willing to take the fall for Penney and admit to killing Hillier-Penney.

"In order for that to be effective, it was intimated to Mr. Penney that he would have to honestly disclose exactly what happened so that Ryan’s confession would match the forensics," Khaladkar said. "The crime boss needed to know everything that happened, including the particulars of the disposal of the body."
Hear the moment Dean Penney tells undercover police about death of Jennifer Hillier Penney

The defence argued Penney was intimidated by the fictitious crime boss during the first interview, which took place on a yacht in Vancouver harbour. Penney was being interviewed for a job as the yacht's captain.
Khaladkar did not find there were any threats.
7. Personal characteristics of the accused
Penney only had a Grade 8 education, but Khaladkar said he wasn't convinced his lack of schooling made him "intellectually limited or unusually vulnerable."
The court was told Penney completed courses at the Marine Institute and obtained a mariner captain's certificate.
There was also evidence he was aware of Mr. Big stings. Before his first confession, Penney expressed concern someone could "walk in through here and whack the cuffs on me."
"Mr. Penney is not unsophisticated," Khaladkar wrote.
The decision

Khaladkar found Penney's confession provided several details that were not publicly known, which strengthened the Crown's argument that the probative value of the information outweighed the prejudicial nature of the investigation.

The prejudice, Khaladkar wrote, was presenting a side of Penney to the jury that showed a man who was willing to participate in organized criminal activity such as smuggling weapons, stealing fuel tankers and moving stolen diamonds.

"But that prejudice can be managed by proper instructions and by careful control over what aspects of the operation are actually placed before the jury," Khaladkar wrote. "It can also be managed by ensuring that the jury sees only a representative number of scenarios."

items: Guns, jewels and a heist: Inside the fake world police built for accused killer Dean Penney
How an undercover officer became Dean Penney's best friend after his wife disappeared

blocks.text: For example, Khaladkar wrote: "It is not necessary to place each and every scenario before the jury, particularly the one in which Mr. Penney confessed to UC-Vic that he had, in a fit of rage, used a hammer on a ram that had butted him. That aspect of the operation would likely carry disproportionate prejudicial effect and need not be led."

With those seven boxes checked, the judge moved to the final hurdle: whether or not the operation amounted to an abuse of process. The defence never claimed it did, but Khaladkar formally ruled it did not.

"The evidence given by Mr. Penney does not displace the strong showing made by the Crown, on a balance of probabilities, that the accused’s confession to the crime boss is reliable and therefore admissible," he said. "Whether the confession is ultimately accepted, and the weight to be given to it, are matters for the jury."
The jury deliberated for parts of five days in May, before returning with a guilty verdict.
Penney was sentenced last week, receiving the mandatory life sentence without parole eligibility for 25 years.
When asked if he had anything to say, Penney proclaimed his innocence and said he hopes "to be vindicated soon."

articles.title: EU announces plan to restrict social media access for children
articles.summary: Under the plans, only children over 15 would be able to set up their own social media accounts.

blocks.text: The EU has announced plans to restrict social media access for under-16s across its member states, in a bid to increase wellbeing and tackle online safety.
Under the plans, there would be a gradual approach to children using social media which would include banning under 13s from accessing platforms.
Those aged 13 to 15 would only be able to access platforms for an hour per day via "mini accounts" set up through their parent or guardian's social media account.

The European Commission said social media companies would need to prove their platforms were safe by design, while EU chief Ursula von der Leyen said the move would "put parents back in the driving seat".
She added the legislation - called the EU Kids Act - would give parents "the tools to help their children navigate a safer world".
Under the act, only children aged 15 and over would be able to set up their own social media accounts.
Von der Leyen has previously proposed a social media "delay" for children in Europe, saying in May that "the discussion about a minimum age for social media can no longer be ignored".
The policy, formally outlined on Thursday, was also trailed in the EU chief's annual address to the EU Parliament on Wednesday.
Some individual EU countries have already announced their own separate plans to restrict social media for children, including France and Spain.

articles.title: Uncontrolled AI could lead to 'silicon species' rivalling humans, warns Microsoft
articles.summary: Mustafa Suleyman says he believes rival AI firm Anthropic is in effect teaching Claude it "may be conscious".

blocks.text: Speaking to the Today programme on Thursday, Suleyman warned against firms continuing to create AI systems capable of setting their own objectives, earning money and owning assets.
That would mean "essentially seeding a new silicon species", he said, which could "no doubt compete with us for resources, no matter how much it cares about humanity and loves us".

Suleyman's comments to the BBC follow an essay he published earlier this week, external, in which he questioned Anthropic's approach to training its AI model Claude, despite praising boss Dario Amodei and his team as "intellectually honest people".

In it, he criticised Anthropic for teaching its AI to have human-like qualities, a practice known as anthropomorphising, which he said made it seem as though Claude had its own desires, values and sense of self.
He also warned tech firms risk creating something "impossible" to control by treating the technology like a human.
"AIs are not conscious," he wrote.
"They do not feel, experience, or suffer. They do not have innate preferences or underlying motivations.
"They are sequence completion engines, internally hollow, designed to follow instructions, and accomplish goals set by humans."
The question of how much autonomy AI systems should have is increasingly dividing the industry.
Speaking to the BBC about an upcoming AI summit, Suleyman called for "alignment" to create technology that must be "subordinate" to humanity.
Alignment is a field which aims to build human ethical ideas and principles into AI. In other words, it aims to keep it on track with what humans value.

"I think that the good news here is that everybody who is human is going to have a very strong interest in making sure that the systems that we all create and... are used around the world in every nation are safe and controllable and subordinate to humanity," he said.
"Everybody must be aligned."
Microsoft founded its own superintelligence team in October 2025 and the company, much like its rival Anthropic, is also pursuing efforts in advanced AI development.

Suleyman's comments reflects Microsoft's initial draft of its Humanist AI Code of Conduct, external, a "training manual" published on Monday for how the company is developing its AI, which sets out the idea of "humanist superintelligence".
This, the code states, is "very advanced AI that always works for people, stays within limits, and remains under human control".
The company's vision of a "humanist" AI highlights the central challenge facing the technology - how to make it more powerful, without losing sight of the values it is meant to serve.
Additional reporting by Henry Moore

articles.title: Palace leaves impeachment vote threshold to Senate
articles.summary: The Palace backed the former Supreme Court justices' view that the decision on the voting threshold for convicting Vice President Sara Duterte lies solely with Senate impeachment court.

blocks.text: September 17, 2026 | 4:14pm
Retired Chief Justice Artemio Panganiban presented his views on the voting threshold issue during his appearance before the Senate impeachment court as one of the amici curiae, September 16, 2026.
Senate of the Philippines

MANILA, Philippines — Malacañang said Thursday, September 17, that it would stay out of the Senate impeachment court’s deliberations on the number of votes needed to convict Vice President Sara Duterte in her impeachment case.

Palace Press Officer Claire Castro made the statement following the appearance of former members of the Supreme Court in the Senate impeachment court on Wednesday, September 16, to help resolve the voting threshold issue.

“Muli, ang Palasyo ay hindi po manghihimasok kung ano man po ang sasabihin or magiging desisyon ng Senado dahil malinaw naman po ang sinabi ng mga justices natin. Dapat ito ay para sa katotohanan. Truth, fairness and justice,” Castro said in a press briefing.
(Again, the Palace will not intervene in the decisions of the Senate because our justices have made it clear already that the decision must be for truth. Truth, fairness and justice.)

Retired chief justices Artemio Panganiban and Reynato Puno, including retired Supreme Court associate justice Adolfo Azcuna, personally appeared before the Senate impeachment court on Wednesday as amici curiae, or friends of the court, to answer questions from senator-judges.
Retired Chief Justice Hilario Davide Jr., meanwhile, sent a memorandum containing his views on the voting threshold issue.

“Naging maganda po ang naging talakayan ng mga amici curiae sa nasabing conference dahil mas naliwanagan ang taong-bayan. Naliwanagan din po siguro ang mga maraming mga mambabatas patungkol sa issue sa threshold,” Castro said.
(The discussion among the amici curiae during the conference went well, because it helped clarify the issue for the public. It may have also helped many lawmakers with the threshold issue.)
Senate’s decision
The senator-judges tapped the help of former justices to resolve what the constitutional rule on the required “two-thirds of all members of the Senate” for conviction means.

The Senate impeachment court is trying to determine whether the rule covers the entire 24 elected senators, or only those who are actively participating in the trial, excluding those who are jailed, out of the country, or in hiding.
While Panganiban, Puno, and Davide expressed that the rule must not be interpreted literally, Azcuna said the rule means 16 votes out of the 24 senator-judges are needed for conviction.
The chief justices, however, said the Senate impeachment court has the “sole power” to decide on the voting threshold issue.
This was backed by the Palace, saying that any decision that will come up from the senator-judges’ differing interpretations of the rule no longer concerns the administration.

“Hindi po nangangamba ang Palasyo dahil kahit ano po ang kanilang maging opinyon diyan, ‘yan po ang kanilang magiging pagpapasya. So kung ano po ang mangyayari sa Senado, nasa kanilang responsibilidad 'yan; wala po sa administrasyon,” Castro said.
(The Palace is not concerned, because whatever their opinions will be, those will be their decisions. So whatever happens in the senate, that’s their responsibility, not the administration’s.)

articles.title: FACT CHECK: No lockdown in Malacañang after court ordered VP Sara’s arrest
articles.summary: No credible reports confirm that barricades and barbed wire were installed around Malacañang due to the issuance of Duterte's arrest warrant, contrary to the claim

blocks.text: Claim: Malacañang was placed under lockdown following the issuance of an arrest warrant against Vice President Sara Duterte.

Why we fact-checked this: The video bearing the claim has already received 648,000 views, 26,000 reacts, 2,600 shares, and 1,400 comments as of writing. It was posted on September 6, days after a Quezon City trial court issued an arrest warrant against the Vice President.

The video shows a photo of Duterte on her arrival at the Quezon City court to post bail. Images of President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., his mother Imelda Marcos, and Ilocos Norte 1st District Representative Sandro Marcos can also be seen in the video’s graphics.

The narrator of the Facebook reel says, “Sa kabila po ng pag-aresto kay VP Sara, nag-lockdown ang Malacañang. Opo, nagkaroon na naman po ng barikada, ng mga barbed wire ang Malacañang, mga kababayan, kasunod ng pag-aresto kay VP Sara, kasunod ng paglabas ng warrant of arrest kay VP Sara.”

(Following the arrest of VP Sara, Malacañang went into lockdown. Yes, barricades and barbed wires have once again been set up at Malacañang following the arrest of VP Sara, following the issuance of the arrest warrant against her.)
Some Facebook users believed the claim. One comment reads, “Lumalabas na sila takot. For the first time, siya lang nag lockdown na Presidente.”
(It turns out they are afraid. For the first time, he was the only president to impose a lockdown).

The facts: Malacañang has not imposed a lockdown following the issuance of Duterte’s arrest warrant on September 4 and her posting of bail on September 5. No credible reports confirm that barricades and barbed wire have been installed around the area.

The Palace has previously implemented heightened security measures due to rallies such as the September 2025 and November 2025 anti-corruption rallies as well as the July 2026 protest by the United People’s Initiative.

More recently, police conducted a simulation exercise and installed metal barricades and razor wire on roads leading to the Malacañang Complex as preparation for National Heroes Day activities on August 31.
Following the issuance of Duterte’s arrest warrant, several supporters gathered at the Quezon City court on September 5 and on September 11 for her arraignment, which was later deferred.

Grave threats case: The warrant of arrest against Duterte was issued after the Quezon City Regional Trial Court Branch 98 found probable cause to hold the Vice President for trial on three counts of grave threats.

The case stemmed from Duterte’s November 2024 warning that she allegedly hired an assassin to kill President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., First Lady Liza Araneta-Marcos, and former House speaker Martin Romualdez.
The Vice President posted bail of P360,000 — P120,000 for each count.

On the same day she posted bail, Duterte said that she does not feel safe, citing previous alleged security threats. “I do not feel safe. I do not feel safe anywhere. Pumunta lang ako [rito] kasi sabi ninyo pupunta ako sa court (I only went here because you told me I needed to appear in court),” she said.

Interior Secretary Jonvic Remulla told the media that they accorded Duterte the respect “that her position deserves.” He added, “We have all the body cam footages of her warrants being served. We have all the body cam footages of her arrival to post bail.”
Previous fact checks: Rappler has previously fact-checked similar false claims about the Vice President:
